plain_english_summary: Sets the core registrability bar: a mark (including a product or app name) cannot be registered if it is purely generic, merely descriptive of the goods/service, or has become a common trade term - unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use or is well-known. Software founders picking a purely descriptive product name (e.g. 'Cloud Storage') risk exactly this refusal.

chapter_title: THE REGISTER AND CONDITIONS FOR REGISTRATION
title: Limitation as to colour
text: (1) A trade mark may be limited wholly or in part to any combination of colours and any such limitation shall be taken into consideration by the Registrar or the High Court, as the case may be, having to decide on the distinctive character of the trade mark.

sub_structure.2: (2) So far as a trade mark is registered without limitation of colour, it shall be deemed to be registered for all colours.

plain_english_summary: An applicant can register a mark limited to specific colours (relevant for brand colour palettes/logos), and a mark registered without any colour limitation is treated as covering all colours.

chapter_title: THE REGISTER AND CONDITIONS FOR REGISTRATION
title: Relative grounds for refusal of registration
text: (1) Save as provided in section 12, a trade mark shall not be registered if, because of- (a) its identity with an earlier trade mark and similarity of goods or services covered by the trade mark; or (b) its similarity to an earlier trade mark and the identity or similarity of the goods or services covered by the trade mark, there exists a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, which includes the likelihood of association with the earlier trade mark.

sub_structure.2: (2) A trade mark which is identical with or similar to an earlier well-known trade mark shall not be registered for dissimilar goods or services if the use of the later mark without due cause would take unfair advantage of, or be detrimental to, the distinctive character or repute of the earlier well-known mark.
sub_structure.3: (3) A trade mark shall not be registered if, or to the extent that, its use in India is liable to be prevented by virtue of the law of passing off protecting an unregistered trade mark, or by virtue of the law of copyright.
sub_structure.4: (4) Nothing in this section shall prevent registration where the proprietor of the earlier trade mark or other earlier right consents to the registration.
sub_structure.5: (5) A trade mark shall not be refused registration on the grounds in sub-sections (2) and (3) unless objection is raised in opposition proceedings by the proprietor of the earlier trade mark.

plain_english_summary: Bars registration of a new mark that is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered/well-known mark for the same or related goods/services, and also protects unregistered marks via passing-off and copyright - the core 'can I actually use this brand name' search-and-clearance provision every software startup should check before adopting a name.

chapter_title: THE REGISTER AND CONDITIONS FOR REGISTRATION
title: Registration in the case of honest concurrent use, etc.
text: In the case of honest concurrent use or of other special circumstances which in the opinion of the Registrar, make it proper so to do, he may permit the registration by more than one proprietor of the trade marks which are identical or similar (whether any such trade mark is already registered or not) in respect of the same or similar goods or services, subject to such conditions and limitations, if any, as the Registrar may think fit to impose.
plain_english_summary: Allows two unrelated businesses to each register the same or a similar mark if their historical, good-faith concurrent use justifies it - an exception to the usual bar on confusingly similar marks.

chapter_title: THE REGISTER AND CONDITIONS FOR REGISTRATION
title: Prohibition of registration of names of chemical elements or international non-proprietary names
text: No word- (a) which is the commonly used and accepted name of any single chemical element or any single chemical compound in respect of a chemical substance or preparation, or (b) which is declared by the World Health Organisation and notified in the prescribed manner by the Registrar from time to time, as an international non-proprietary name or which is deceptively similar to such name, shall be registered as a trade mark and any such registration shall be deemed for the purpose of section 57 to be an entry made in the register without sufficient cause or an entry wrongly remaining on the register, as the circumstances may require.
plain_english_summary: Blocks registration of generic chemical-element/compound names and WHO-designated international non-proprietary (drug) names as trade marks, and treats any such registration as invalid and liable to be struck off.

chapter_title: THE REGISTER AND CONDITIONS FOR REGISTRATION
title: Use of names and representations of living persons or persons recently dead
text: Where an application is made for the registration of a trade mark which falsely suggests a connection with any living person, or a person whose death took place within twenty years prior to the date of application for registration of the trade mark, the Registrar may, before he proceeds with the application, require the applicant to furnish him with the consent in writing of such living person or, as the case may be, of the legal representative of the deceased person to the connection appearing on the trade mark, and may refuse to proceed with the application unless the applicant furnishes the Registrar with such consent.
plain_english_summary: If a proposed mark implies an endorsement or connection with a living person (or someone who died within the last 20 years), the Registrar can demand written consent from that person or their legal representative before registering it - relevant to naming a product or feature after a real individual.

chapter_title: THE REGISTER AND CONDITIONS FOR REGISTRATION
title: Registration of parts of trade marks and of trade marks as a series
text: (1) Where the proprietor of a trade mark claims to be entitled to the exclusive use of any part thereof separately, he may apply to register the whole and the part as separate trade marks.

sub_structure.3: (3) Where a person claiming to be the proprietor of several trade marks in respect of the same or similar goods or services, resembling each other in material particulars but differing in respect of statement of goods/services, numbers, price, quality, names of places, other non-distinctive matter, or colour, seeks to register those trade marks, they may be registered as a series in one registration.

plain_english_summary: Lets a business register a logo/mark and a distinctive sub-part of it separately, or register a family of closely related marks (differing only in minor, non-distinctive respects) together as a 'series' in a single application - useful for product-line branding.

chapter_title: THE REGISTER AND CONDITIONS FOR REGISTRATION
title: Registration of trade marks as associated trade marks
text: (1) Where a trade mark which is registered, or is the subject of an application for registration, in respect of any goods or services is identical with another trade mark which is registered, or is the subject of an application for registration, in the name of the same proprietor in respect of the same or nearly resembling goods or services, or so nearly resembles it as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion if used by a person other than the proprietor, the Registrar may, at any time, require that the trade marks shall be entered on the register as associated trade marks.

sub_structure.5: (5) On application by the registered proprietor of two or more trade marks registered as associated trade marks, the Registrar may dissolve the association if satisfied there would be no likelihood of deception or confusion if that trade mark were used by any other person.

plain_english_summary: Where the same owner holds multiple identical or confusingly similar marks, the Registrar links them on the register as 'associated' marks (which, per section 44, must then be assigned together) - the Registrar can later dissolve that linkage if it's no longer needed.

chapter_title: THE REGISTER AND CONDITIONS FOR REGISTRATION
title: Effect of registration of parts of a mark
text: (1) When a trade mark consists of several matters, its registration shall confer on the proprietor exclusive right to the use of the trade mark taken as a whole.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where a trade mark contains a part that is not separately registered, or contains matter common to the trade or otherwise non-distinctive, the registration does not confer any exclusive right in that part standing alone.

plain_english_summary: Registering a composite mark (e.g. a logo plus tagline) protects the whole combination, but does not automatically give exclusive rights over a generic or undistinctive element used within it.

chapter_title: PROCEDURE FOR AND DURATION OF REGISTRATION
title: Application for registration
text: (1) Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used or proposed to be used by him, who is desirous of registering it, shall apply in writing to the Registrar in the prescribed manner for the registration of his trade mark.

sub_structure.2: (2) A single application may be made for registration of a trade mark for different classes of goods and services and fee payable therefor shall be in respect of each such class of goods or services.
sub_structure.4: (4) Subject to the provisions of this Act, the Registrar may refuse the application or may accept it absolutely or subject to such amendments, modifications, conditions or limitations, if any, as he may think fit.
sub_structure.5: (5) In the case of a refusal or conditional acceptance of an application, the Registrar shall record in writing the grounds for such refusal or conditional acceptance.

plain_english_summary: Sets out the basic application process for registering a trade mark, including that one multi-class application can cover several classes of goods/services (each attracting its own fee) - the starting point for any software company's trademark filing.

chapter_title: PROCEDURE FOR AND DURATION OF REGISTRATION
title: Withdrawal of acceptance
text: Where, after the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark but before its registration, the Registrar is satisfied that the application has been accepted in error, or that the trade mark should not be registered or should be registered subject to different conditions, the Registrar may, after hearing the applicant if he so desires, withdraw the acceptance and proceed as if the application had not been accepted.
plain_english_summary: Gives the Registrar a safety valve to reopen and reconsider an application that was mistakenly accepted, before final registration.

chapter_title: PROCEDURE FOR AND DURATION OF REGISTRATION
title: Advertisement of application
text: (1) When an application for registration of a trade mark has been accepted, whether absolutely or subject to conditions or limitations, the Registrar shall, as soon as may be after acceptance, cause the application as accepted to be advertised in the prescribed manner.

sub_structure.proviso: Provided that the Registrar may cause the application to be advertised before acceptance if it relates to a trade mark to which section 9(1) or section 11(1)/(2) apply, or where expedient by reason of exceptional circumstances.

plain_english_summary: Accepted trade mark applications are published in the official Trade Marks Journal, opening a window for third parties to oppose the registration.

chapter_title: PROCEDURE FOR AND DURATION OF REGISTRATION
title: Opposition to registration
text: (1) Any person may, within four months from the date of the advertisement or re-advertisement of an application for registration, give notice in writing in the prescribed manner and on payment of such fee as may be prescribed, to the Registrar, of opposition to the registration.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Registrar shall serve a copy of the notice on the applicant, who must within two months send a counterstatement of the grounds relied on, failing which he is deemed to have abandoned the application.
sub_structure.5: (5) The Registrar shall, after hearing the parties if required and considering the evidence, decide whether and subject to what conditions the registration is to be permitted.

plain_english_summary: Any third party (e.g. a competitor who thinks a proposed brand clashes with their own) has four months from advertisement to formally oppose a trade mark application, triggering a counterstatement-and-evidence process before the Registrar decides.

chapter_title: PROCEDURE FOR AND DURATION OF REGISTRATION
title: Correction and amendment
text: The Registrar may, on such terms as he thinks just, at any time, whether before or after acceptance of an application for registration under section 18, permit the correction of any error in or in connection with the application or permit an amendment of the application.

sub_structure.proviso: Provided that if an amendment involves dividing a multi-class application into two or more applications, the date of the initial application is deemed to be the date of the divided applications.

plain_english_summary: Allows applicants to fix errors or amend a pending application, and preserves the original filing date even if a multi-class application is later split into separate applications.

chapter_title: PROCEDURE FOR AND DURATION OF REGISTRATION
title: Registration
text: (1) Subject to the provisions of section 19, when an application for registration of a trade mark has been accepted and either the application has not been opposed and the time for notice of opposition has expired, or the opposition has been decided in favour of the applicant, the Registrar shall, unless the Central Government otherwise directs, register the said trade mark within eighteen months of the filing of the application and the trade mark when registered shall be registered as of the date of the making of the said application.

sub_structure.2: (2) On registration, the Registrar shall issue to the applicant a certificate in the prescribed form, sealed with the seal of the Trade Marks Registry.
sub_structure.3: (3) Where registration is not completed within twelve months from the date of application by reason of default of the applicant, the Registrar may treat the application as abandoned after notice.

plain_english_summary: Once an unopposed or successfully defended application clears, the Registrar must register the mark within eighteen months of filing, backdated to the original filing date - and issues a registration certificate as proof of ownership.

chapter_title: PROCEDURE FOR AND DURATION OF REGISTRATION
title: Jointly owned trade marks
text: (1) Save as provided in sub-section (2), nothing in this Act shall authorise the registration of two or more persons who use a trade mark independently, or propose so to use it, as joint proprietors thereof.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where the relations between two or more persons are such that no one of them is entitled to use the mark except on behalf of both/all of them, or in relation to goods/services with which both/all of them are connected, those persons may be registered as joint proprietors, and the Act operates as if their combined rights vested in a single person.

plain_english_summary: Two founders/entities cannot register the same mark as independent co-owners who each use it on their own account, but can be registered as joint proprietors if they only ever use the mark jointly on behalf of both of them.

chapter_title: PROCEDURE FOR AND DURATION OF REGISTRATION
title: Duration, renewal, removal and restoration of registration
text: (1) The registration of a trade mark, after the commencement of this Act, shall be for a period of ten years, but may be renewed from time to time in accordance with the provisions of this section.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Registrar shall, on application by the registered proprietor within the prescribed period and on payment of the prescribed fee, renew the registration for a further period of ten years.
sub_structure.3: (3) The Registrar shall notify the proprietor before expiry; if renewal conditions are not met the Registrar may remove the mark from the register, unless a late renewal application with surcharge is filed within six months of expiry.
sub_structure.4: (4) A mark removed for non-payment can be restored within one year of expiry, on application and fee, if the Registrar is satisfied it is just to do so.

plain_english_summary: Trade mark registration lasts ten years and is indefinitely renewable in further ten-year blocks - a recurring compliance/calendar item every SaaS company's legal-ops needs to track, with a grace/restoration window if a renewal deadline is missed.

chapter_title: PROCEDURE FOR AND DURATION OF REGISTRATION
title: Effect of removal from register for failure to pay fee for renewal
text: Where a trade mark has been removed from the register for failure to pay the fee for renewal, it shall nevertheless, for the purpose of any application for the registration of another trade mark during one year next after the date of removal, be deemed to be a trade mark already on the register, unless the Registrar or the High Court, as the case may be, is satisfied that there was no bona fide trade use of the mark during the two years before removal, or that no deception or confusion would arise from the new application.
plain_english_summary: Even after a mark lapses for non-renewal, it still blocks new confusingly similar applications for one year, as a cooling-off period - unless it's shown the old mark wasn't genuinely used or there's no real confusion risk.

title: No action for infringement of unregistered trade mark
text: (1) No person shall be entitled to institute any proceeding to prevent, or to recover damages for, the infringement of an unregistered trade mark.

sub_structure.2: (2) Nothing in this Act shall be deemed to affect rights of action against any person for passing off goods or services as the goods of another person or as services provided by another person, or the remedies in respect thereof.

plain_english_summary: You cannot sue for 'infringement' of an unregistered brand under this Act - but the common-law action of passing off remains available, which is why software startups are usually advised to register their brand rather than rely solely on use-based rights.

title: Rights conferred by registration
text: (1) Subject to the other provisions of this Act, the registration of a trade mark shall, if valid, give to the registered proprietor of the trade mark the exclusive right to the use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered and to obtain relief in respect of infringement of the trade mark in the manner provided by this Act.

sub_structure.2: (2) The exclusive right to use is subject to any conditions and limitations to which the registration is subject.
sub_structure.3: (3) Where two or more persons are registered proprietors of identical or nearly resembling trade marks, neither acquires exclusive rights against the other merely by registration; each has the same rights against third parties as if he were the sole proprietor.

plain_english_summary: This is the core payoff of registering a trade mark: exclusive nationwide rights to use the mark for the registered goods/services and the right to sue for infringement - subject to whatever conditions or limitations were placed on the registration.

title: Infringement of registered trade marks
text: (1) A registered trade mark is infringed by a person who, not being a registered proprietor or a person using by way of permitted use, uses in the course of trade, a mark which is identical with, or deceptively similar to, the trade mark in relation to goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered and in such manner as to render the use of the mark likely to be taken as being used as a trade mark.

sub_structure.2: (2) It is also infringement where a mark's identity/similarity to the registered mark, combined with identity/similarity of goods or services, is likely to cause confusion or an association with the registered mark on the part of the public.
sub_structure.4: (4) It is infringement to use an identical/similar mark on dissimilar goods or services where the registered mark has a reputation in India and the use, without due cause, takes unfair advantage of or is detrimental to its distinctive character or repute (dilution).
sub_structure.5: (5) A registered trade mark is infringed by a person who uses it as his trade name or as part of the name of his business concern dealing in the goods or services for which the mark is registered.
sub_structure.6: (6) A person 'uses' a mark if he affixes it to goods/packaging, offers or stocks goods or supplies services under it, imports/exports goods under it, or uses it on business papers or in advertising.
sub_structure.8: (8) A registered trade mark is infringed by any advertising of it that takes unfair advantage and is contrary to honest commercial practices, is detrimental to its distinctive character, or is against its reputation (comparative-advertising abuse).

plain_english_summary: Defines what counts as trademark infringement: using an identical/confusingly similar mark on the same or related goods/services, diluting a reputed mark even on unrelated goods, or using someone else's mark as your company/trade name - this is the section a software company's brand-enforcement and clearance strategy is built around, and also what a company must avoid when naming its own product, domain, or business entity.

title: Limits on effect of registered trade mark
text: (1) Nothing in section 29 shall be construed as preventing the use of a registered trade mark by any person for the purposes of identifying goods or services as those of the proprietor provided the use is in accordance with honest practices in industrial or commercial matters, and is not such as to take unfair advantage of or be detrimental to the distinctive character or repute of the trade mark.

sub_structure.2: (2) A registered trade mark is not infringed by: descriptive use indicating the kind, quality, purpose, geographical origin etc. of goods/services; use within the conditions/limitations of a registration; use by a person connected in the course of trade with the proprietor/registered user where goods bearing the mark have been genuinely put on the market; or use indicating that goods/services are compatible/adapted accessories.
sub_structure.3: (3) Once goods bearing a registered mark are lawfully acquired, their further resale or dealing is not infringement merely because the mark was later assigned, or because the goods were put on the market by the proprietor or with his consent (exhaustion of rights).
sub_structure.4: (4) Sub-section (3) does not apply where the proprietor has legitimate reasons to oppose further dealing, e.g. where the condition of the goods has changed or been impaired after being put on the market.

plain_english_summary: Carves out important defences to infringement: honest referential/comparative use, descriptive use, compatible-accessory labelling ('works with X'), and exhaustion of rights once goods are lawfully sold - relevant to how a SaaS product can legitimately reference a competitor's or integration partner's trade mark (e.g. 'integrates with Slack').

title: Registration to be prima facie evidence of validity
text: (1) In all legal proceedings relating to a trade mark registered under this Act (including applications under section 57), the original registration of the trade mark and of all subsequent assignments and transmissions of the trade mark shall be prima facie evidence of the validity thereof.

sub_structure.2: (2) A registered trade mark shall not be held invalid on the ground that it was not registrable under section 9 except upon evidence of distinctiveness not submitted before registration, if it is proved the mark had become distinctive by the date of registration.

plain_english_summary: A trade mark certificate is treated as prima facie proof that the registration (and any assignment chain) is valid, shifting the evidentiary burden onto a party challenging it.

title: Protection of registration on ground of distinctiveness in certain cases
text: Where a trade mark is registered in breach of sub-section (1) of section 9, it shall not be declared invalid if, in consequence of the use which has been made of it, it has after registration and before commencement of any legal proceedings challenging the validity of such registration, acquired a distinctive character in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered.
plain_english_summary: Even a mark that should not have been registered for lack of distinctiveness can be saved from invalidation if it has since become genuinely distinctive through use, before any court challenge begins.

title: Effect of acquiescence
text: (1) Where the proprietor of an earlier trade mark has acquiesced for a continuous period of five years in the use of a registered trade mark, being aware of that use, he shall no longer be entitled on the basis of that earlier trade mark to apply for a declaration that the registration of the later trade mark is invalid, or to oppose its use, unless the registration of the later trade mark was not applied for in good faith.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where sub-section (1) applies, the proprietor of the later trade mark is correspondingly not entitled to oppose the use of the earlier trade mark.

plain_english_summary: If an earlier trade mark owner knowingly tolerates a later, similar registered mark for five straight years, they lose the right to challenge it (unless the later mark was filed in bad faith) - a 'use it or lose the objection' rule that rewards prompt enforcement.

title: Saving for vested rights
text: Nothing in this Act shall entitle the proprietor or a registered user of registered trade mark to interfere with or restrain the use by any person of a trade mark identical with or nearly resembling it in relation to goods or services in relation to which that person or a predecessor in title has continuously used that trade mark from a date prior to the first use or registration of the first-mentioned trade mark, whichever is earlier.
plain_english_summary: Protects a genuine prior user of a mark from being shut down by someone who later registered an identical or similar mark - prior continuous use trumps later registration.

title: Saving for use of name, address or description of goods or services
text: Nothing in this Act shall entitle the proprietor or a registered user of a registered trade mark to interfere with any bona fide use by a person of his own name or that of his place of business, or the name of any of his predecessors in business, or the use by any person of any bona fide description of the character or quality of his goods or services.
plain_english_summary: Registering a trade mark cannot stop someone else from honestly using their own personal/business name, or from honestly describing the nature or quality of their own goods or services.

title: Saving for words used as name or description of an article or substance or service
text: (1) The registration of a trade mark shall not be deemed to have become invalid by reason only of any use after the date of registration of any word which the trade mark contains as the name or description of an article, substance or service, unless it is shown that the word has become the well-known and established name of that article/substance/service among traders (other than the proprietor/registered user), or that a formerly patented article's only practicable name is that word two years after the patent expired.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where such genericide is proved, the trade mark rights over the word cease as regards that article/substance/service, either for purposes of a rectification action under section 57 or for other legal proceedings.

plain_english_summary: Addresses trade mark 'genericide' - if a registered mark's word becomes the actual generic name traders use for that kind of article or service (the classic risk for a wildly successful product name), the owner can lose exclusive rights over that word for that product category.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO PROTECTION OF TRADE MARKS THROUGH INTERNATIONAL REGISTRATION UNDER THE MADRID PROTOCOL
title: Application of Act in case of international registration under Madrid Protocol
text: The provisions of this Chapter shall apply to international applications and international registrations under the Madrid Protocol.
plain_english_summary: Confirms that this special chapter governs how the Madrid Protocol's international trade mark registration system interacts with Indian law - the mechanism a software company can use to extend its Indian trade mark into 100+ other Madrid Protocol member countries through one filing.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO PROTECTION OF TRADE MARKS THROUGH INTERNATIONAL REGISTRATION UNDER THE MADRID PROTOCOL
title: Definitions
text: In this Chapter, unless the context otherwise requires,-

sub_structure.b: "basic application" means an application for the registration of a trade mark filed under section 18 and which is used as a basis for applying for an international registration;
sub_structure.c: "basic registration" means the registration of a trade mark under section 23 and which is used as a basis for applying for an international registration;
sub_structure.h: "international application" means an application for international registration or for extension of the protection resulting from an international registration to any Contracting Party made under the Madrid Protocol;
sub_structure.j: "international registration" means the registration of a trade mark in the register of the International Bureau effected under the Madrid Protocol;
sub_structure.l: "Madrid Protocol" means the Protocol relating to the Madrid Agreement Concerning the International Registration of Marks adopted at Madrid on the 27th day of June, 1989, as amended from time to time.

plain_english_summary: Defines the Madrid Protocol-specific vocabulary - 'basic application/registration' (the Indian filing a company must already hold), 'international application', and 'international registration' - needed to understand the international filing route in sections 36C-36G.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO PROTECTION OF TRADE MARKS THROUGH INTERNATIONAL REGISTRATION UNDER THE MADRID PROTOCOL
title: Trade Marks Registry to deal with international applications
text: Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (3) of section 5, an international application shall be dealt with by the head office of the Trade Marks Registry or such branch office of the Registry, as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify.
plain_english_summary: Designates which office of the Indian Trade Marks Registry handles international (Madrid Protocol) applications.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO PROTECTION OF TRADE MARKS THROUGH INTERNATIONAL REGISTRATION UNDER THE MADRID PROTOCOL
title: International application originating from India
text: (1) Where an application for the registration of a trade mark has been made under section 18 or a trade mark has been registered under section 23, the applicant or the registered proprietor may make an international application on the form prescribed by the Common Regulations for international registration of that trade mark.

sub_structure.4: (4) The Registrar shall certify that the particulars in the international application correspond to the Indian basic application/registration, and forward the international application to the International Bureau for registration within the prescribed period.
sub_structure.5: (5) If, within five years of the international registration, the underlying Indian basic application or registration is withdrawn, cancelled, expires, or is finally refused (in whole or part), the resulting international protection ceases to have effect for the corresponding goods or services (the 'central attack' rule).

plain_english_summary: Lets an Indian trade mark applicant or owner use their existing Indian filing as the springboard for a Madrid Protocol international application - but for the first five years, the international registration remains dependent on the Indian 'basic' application/registration surviving (central attack), so a software company expanding a brand abroad via Madrid should keep its Indian filing defensible.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO PROTECTION OF TRADE MARKS THROUGH INTERNATIONAL REGISTRATION UNDER THE MADRID PROTOCOL
title: International registrations where India has been designated
text: (1) The Registrar shall, after receipt of an advice from the International Bureau about any international registration where India has been designated, keep a record of the particulars of that international registration in the prescribed manner.

sub_structure.2: (2) If the Registrar is satisfied that protection should not be granted in India, or should be granted only subject to conditions, he may, after hearing the applicant if desired, refuse protection and inform the International Bureau within eighteen months.
sub_structure.4: (4) Sections 9 to 21, 63 and 74 apply mutatis mutandis to an international registration designating India as if it were an application for registration under section 18 (i.e. it goes through the same absolute/relative grounds examination and opposition process).
sub_structure.6: (6) Where a registered proprietor of an Indian trade mark later obtains an international registration designating India, the international registration replaces the Indian registration from that date, without prejudice to previously acquired rights.

plain_english_summary: Sets out how a foreign trade mark owner's international (Madrid) registration designating India is examined and either granted or refused protection in India - it is put through the same substantive examination (distinctiveness, conflicting marks, opposition) as a normal Indian application.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO PROTECTION OF TRADE MARKS THROUGH INTERNATIONAL REGISTRATION UNDER THE MADRID PROTOCOL
title: Effects of international registration
text: (1) From the date of the international registration of a trade mark where India has been designated, or the date of recording of the extension of protection to India, the protection of the trade mark in India shall be the same as if the trade mark had been registered in India.

sub_structure.2: (2) The indication of classes of goods and services given by the applicant shall not bind the Registrar with regard to the determination of the scope of protection of the trade mark.

plain_english_summary: Once extended to India, an international (Madrid) registration has the same legal effect as a directly-filed Indian registration.

chapter_title: SPECIAL PROVISIONS RELATING TO PROTECTION OF TRADE MARKS THROUGH INTERNATIONAL REGISTRATION UNDER THE MADRID PROTOCOL
title: Duration and renewal of international registration
text: (1) The international registration of a trade mark at the International Bureau shall be for a period of ten years and may be renewed for a period of ten years from the expiry of the preceding period.

sub_structure.2: (2) Subject to payment of a surcharge prescribed by the rules, a grace period of six months shall be allowed for renewal of the international registration.

plain_english_summary: Mirrors the domestic ten-year renewal cycle (section 25) for international Madrid Protocol registrations, with a six-month grace period for late renewal on payment of a surcharge.

title: Power of registered proprietor to assign and give receipts
text: The person for the time being entered in the register as proprietor of a trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and to any rights appearing from the register to be vested in any other person, have power to assign the trade mark, and to give effectual receipts for any consideration for such assignment.
plain_english_summary: Confirms the registered owner's basic power to sell/assign their trade mark and issue a valid receipt for the price paid - the starting point for any brand sale or M&A transaction involving a software company's trade mark.

title: Assignability and transmissibility of registered trade marks
text: Notwithstanding anything in any other law to the contrary, a registered trade mark shall, subject to the provisions of this Chapter, be assignable and transmissible, whether with or without the goodwill of the business concerned and in respect either of all the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered or of some only of those goods or services.
plain_english_summary: A registered trade mark can be sold or transferred separately from the underlying business (with or without goodwill), and can be split so only some of the registered goods/services move with the assignment - important flexibility when a software company sells off one product line's brand while keeping the rest of its business.

title: Assignability and transmissibility of unregistered trade marks
text: An unregistered trade mark may be assigned or transmitted with or without the goodwill of the business concerned.
plain_english_summary: Even an unregistered brand can be bought, sold, or transferred, with or without the goodwill of the business using it.

title: Restriction on assignment or transmission where multiple exclusive rights would be created
text: (1) Notwithstanding anything in sections 38 and 39, a trade mark shall not be assignable or transmissible in a case in which as a result there would subsist exclusive rights in more than one person to the use, in relation to the same or similar/associated goods or services, of nearly resembling or identical trade marks, if the use of the marks in exercise of those rights would be likely to deceive or cause confusion.

sub_structure.2: (2) A proprietor proposing to assign a mark may apply to the Registrar for a certificate confirming the proposed assignment would not create such a conflict, which (subject to appeal) is conclusive if registration of title is applied for within six months.

plain_english_summary: Blocks an assignment that would split a mark between two owners in a way likely to confuse the public (e.g. selling the same brand for the same product line to two different buyers) - a company can pre-clear a proposed assignment by getting a Registrar's certificate.

title: Restriction on assignment or transmission when exclusive rights would be created in different parts of India
text: Notwithstanding anything in sections 38 and 39, a trade mark shall not be assignable or transmissible where it would create an exclusive right in one person to use the mark in one part of India and an exclusive right in another person to use a nearly resembling or identical mark in another part of India, unless the Registrar, on application, approves the assignment as not being contrary to the public interest.
plain_english_summary: Prevents splitting a trade mark geographically within India between two owners (e.g. one owner for North India, another for South India) unless the Registrar pre-approves it as not against the public interest.

title: Conditions for assignment otherwise than in connection with the goodwill of a business
text: Where an assignment of a trade mark, whether registered or unregistered, is made otherwise than in connection with the goodwill of the business in which the mark has been or is used, the assignment shall not take effect unless the assignee, within six months of the assignment (extendable by up to three months), applies to the Registrar for directions on advertising the assignment, and advertises it as directed.

sub_structure.explanation: Explanation.-An assignment limited to some of the registered goods/services along with the goodwill of the business in those goods/services, or an assignment of an export-only mark along with the export business's goodwill, is not treated as an assignment 'without goodwill'.

plain_english_summary: A 'naked' assignment of a brand - sold separately from the goodwill of the business using it, which risks misleading consumers - only becomes legally effective once the assignee applies to the Registrar for directions and advertises the transfer as required; this is a compliance step to watch in any deal that carves a software brand out of the business that built it.

title: Assignability and transmissibility of certification trade marks
text: A certification trade mark shall not be assignable or transmissible otherwise than with the consent of the Registrar, for which application shall be made in writing in the prescribed manner.
plain_english_summary: Certification marks (which vouch for a third-party standard, e.g. an ISO-style compliance mark) can only be transferred with the Registrar's prior consent, reflecting the public-trust function they serve.

title: Assignability and transmissibility of associated trade marks
text: Associated trade marks shall be assignable and transmissible only as a whole and not separately, but, subject to the provisions of this Act, they shall, for all other purposes, be deemed to have been registered as separate trade marks.
plain_english_summary: A family of marks linked on the register as 'associated' trade marks (section 16) must be sold or transferred together as a bundle, not piecemeal, even though they otherwise function as independent registrations.

title: Registration of assignments and transmissions
text: (1) Where a person becomes entitled by assignment or transmission to a registered trade mark, he shall apply in the prescribed manner to the Registrar to register his title, and the Registrar shall, on receipt of the application, register him as the proprietor of the trade mark in respect of the goods or services in respect of which the assignment or transmission has effect, and shall cause particulars of such assignment or transmission to be entered on the register.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence of title only where there is a reasonable doubt about the veracity of any statement or document furnished.
sub_structure.4: (4) Until an application under sub-section (1) has been filed, the assignment or transmission shall be ineffective against a person acquiring a conflicting interest in the registered trade mark without knowledge of the assignment or transmission.

plain_english_summary: After a trade mark changes hands (whether by sale, merger, or licensing-related transfer), the new owner must formally register their title with the Registrar - until that's done, the transfer isn't effective against a good-faith third party who later acquires a conflicting interest, so recording the assignment promptly is essential due diligence in any software brand acquisition.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: Proposed use of trade mark by company to be formed, etc.
text: (1) No application for the registration of a trade mark shall be refused, nor shall permission for such registration be withheld, on the ground only that the applicant does not use or propose to use the trade mark, if the Registrar is satisfied that a company is about to be formed and the applicant intends to assign the trade mark to that company for its use, or that the proprietor intends the mark to be used by a person as a registered user after registration.

sub_structure.3: (3) The Registrar or the High Court, as the case may be, may require the applicant to give security for the costs of any opposition or appeal proceedings in such a case, failing which the application may be treated as abandoned.
sub_structure.4: (4) If the applicant relied on an intention to assign to a to-be-formed company, the registration lapses if that company is not registered as proprietor within the prescribed period (or an extension of up to six months).

plain_english_summary: Lets a founder file a trade mark application before incorporating the operating company, on the basis they intend to assign it to the new entity once formed, or that a future licensee will use it as a registered user - a common pattern where a founder reserves the brand ahead of setting up the corporate structure.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: Removal from register and imposition of limitations on ground of non-use
text: (1) A registered trade mark may be taken off the register in respect of the goods or services for which it is registered, on application by any person aggrieved, on the ground either that it was registered without bona fide intention to use it and has in fact not been used, or that a continuous period of five years (up to three months before the application) has elapsed during which there was no bona fide use of the mark.

sub_structure.proviso: Provided that such an application may be refused if bona fide use is shown for goods/services of the same description, or associated goods/services, even if not the exact registered goods/services.

plain_english_summary: A trade mark that sits unused for five years is vulnerable to being cancelled by any interested party - so a software company must show genuine, ongoing commercial use of its registered marks (including through licensed/registered-user use) to keep them defensible.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: Registered users
text: (1) Subject to the provisions of section 49, a person other than the registered proprietor of a trade mark may be registered as a registered user thereof in respect of any or all of the goods or services in respect of which the trade mark is registered.

sub_structure.2: (2) The permitted use of a trade mark shall be deemed to be used by the proprietor thereof, and shall be deemed not to be used by a person other than the proprietor, for the purposes of section 47 (non-use cancellation) or any other purpose for which such use is material under this Act or any other law.

plain_english_summary: This is the statutory basis for trade mark licensing in India: a licensee can be formally registered as a 'registered user', and their use of the mark counts as use by the owner (protecting the registration from non-use cancellation) while use by an unregistered/unauthorised third party does not - so a SaaS company licensing its brand to a reseller, subsidiary, or franchisee should register that licensee as a registered user.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: Registration as registered user
text: (1) Where it is proposed that a person should be registered as a registered user of a trade mark, the registered proprietor and the proposed registered user shall jointly apply in writing to the Registrar in the prescribed manner, and every such application shall be accompanied by the agreement in writing (or authenticated copy) entered into between them with respect to the permitted use, and an affidavit giving particulars of the relationship (including the degree of quality control the proprietor exercises), the goods/services covered, any conditions or restrictions, and whether the permitted use is time-limited.

sub_structure.1a: (1)(a) requires filing the licensing agreement itself (or an authenticated copy) with the Registrar.
sub_structure.1bi: (1)(b)(i) requires an affidavit giving particulars of the relationship, including the degree of control by the proprietor over the permitted use - i.e. quality-control provisions in the licence.
sub_structure.2: (2) When the requirements of sub-section (1) have been complied with, the Registrar shall register the proposed registered user in respect of the goods or services as to which he is so satisfied.
sub_structure.4: (4) The Registrar shall, if requested, take steps to keep information filed for the application (other than register entries) confidential from trade rivals.

plain_english_summary: Sets out exactly how a trade mark licence is formalised as a registered-user recordal: proprietor and licensee jointly file the licence agreement, plus an affidavit demonstrating the proprietor's quality control over the licensed use - this quality-control showing is central to Indian trademark licensing practice, since a naked licence (no control) risks the mark being treated as abandoned or deceptive; confidential business terms in the licence can be shielded from competitors on request.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: Power of Registrar for variation or cancellation of registration as registered user
text: (1) The registration of a person as registered user may be varied by the Registrar on the proprietor's application; cancelled on application of the proprietor, the registered user, or any other registered user; cancelled on application of any person on grounds including that the registered user used the mark other than in accordance with the licence agreement or in a way causing deception/confusion, that material facts were misrepresented or not disclosed, that circumstances have changed since registration, or that quality-control stipulations in the licence agreement are not being enforced or complied with; or cancelled where the mark is no longer registered for those goods or services.

sub_structure.3: (3) Before cancelling a registration, the registered proprietor shall be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

plain_english_summary: Gives the Registrar broad power to unwind a trademark licence recordal - including, critically, on the ground that quality-control terms in the licensing agreement aren't actually being enforced - which is the regulatory teeth behind the requirement that a trademark licence include real quality control, not just a nominal royalty arrangement.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: Power of Registrar to call for information relating to agreement in respect of registered users
text: (1) The Registrar may, at any time during the continuance of a registered user's registration, by notice in writing, require the registered proprietor to confirm within one month that the licence agreement filed under section 49(1)(a) continues to be in force.

sub_structure.2: (2) If the registered proprietor fails to confirm within one month, the registered user ceases to be a registered user on the day after expiry of that period, and the Registrar shall notify accordingly.

plain_english_summary: The Registrar can periodically demand confirmation that a recorded trademark licence is still live - if the proprietor doesn't respond in time, the registered-user status automatically lapses, so licensors need a process to respond to such Registry notices.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: Right of registered user to take proceedings against infringement
text: (1) Subject to any agreement subsisting between the parties, a registered user may institute proceedings for infringement in his own name as if he were the registered proprietor, making the registered proprietor a defendant, with rights and obligations concurrent with those of the registered proprietor.

sub_structure.2: (2) A registered proprietor so added as defendant shall not be liable for any costs unless he enters an appearance and takes part in the proceedings.

plain_english_summary: A licensee formally recorded as a registered user can sue infringers in its own name (naming the trade mark owner as a co-defendant, who bears no cost risk unless it actively participates) - a valuable enforcement right that flows from proper registered-user recordal, distinct from an unregistered licensee's more limited standing.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: No right of permitted user to take proceeding against infringement
text: A person referred to in sub-clause (ii) of clause (r) of sub-section (1) of section 2 shall have no right to institute any proceeding for any infringement.
plain_english_summary: A 'permitted user' who is not a formally registered user (i.e. someone using the mark merely with the proprietor's written consent, without a registered-user recordal) has no independent right to sue for infringement - reinforcing why formal registered-user recordal matters for a licensee that wants enforcement rights.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: Registered user not to have right of assignment or transmission
text: Nothing in this Act shall confer on a registered user of a trade mark any assignable or transmissible right to the use thereof.

sub_structure.explanation1: Explanation I.-The right of a registered user is not deemed assigned or transmitted where an individual registered user takes on a partner (the firm may keep using the mark only while the original registered user remains a partner), or where a firm registered user undergoes a change in constitution (the reconstituted firm may keep using the mark only while a partner from the time of registration remains a partner).

plain_english_summary: A trademark licence is personal to the registered user and cannot itself be assigned or sub-licensed onward by the licensee - a software licensor should not assume its licensee can pass the licence on to a successor entity without a fresh registered-user application.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: Use of one of associated or substantially identical trade marks equivalent to use of another
text: (1) Where use of a registered trade mark is required to be proved for any purpose, the Registrar or the High Court, as the case may be, may accept use of a registered associated trade mark, or of the trade mark with additions or alterations not substantially affecting its identity, as equivalent to the use required to be proved.

sub_structure.2: (2) The use of the whole of a registered trade mark is deemed to also be use of any part of it that is separately registered under section 15(1) in the name of the same proprietor.

plain_english_summary: Gives some flexibility in proving 'use' of a mark - use of a close variant, an associated mark, or the whole composite mark can count as use of the specific registered mark or its separately-registered part, which matters when a brand's visual presentation evolves over time (e.g. logo refreshes) but the underlying registration needs to stay defensible.

chapter_title: USE OF TRADE MARKS AND REGISTERED USERS
title: Use of trade mark for export trade and use when form of trade connection changes
text: (1) The application in India of a trade mark to goods to be exported from India, or in relation to services for use outside India, and other acts done in India in relation to such exported goods or externally-rendered services which would constitute use of the mark if done for the domestic market, shall be deemed to constitute use of the trade mark for any purpose for which such use is material under this Act or any other law.

sub_structure.2: (2) Use of a registered trade mark by a person connected in trade with the goods/services is not deemed likely to cause confusion merely because a different form of trade connection previously or currently subsists between that person and other goods/services bearing the mark.

plain_english_summary: Confirms that applying a mark to goods/services destined purely for export, or restructuring the trade relationship through which a mark is used (e.g. switching from direct sale to a licensing/franchise model), still counts as valid use of the mark under Indian law.

chapter_title: RECTIFICATION AND CORRECTION OF THE REGISTER
title: Power to cancel or vary registration and to rectify the register
text: (1) On application made in the prescribed manner to the High Court or to the Registrar by any person aggrieved, the Registrar or the High Court, as the case may be, may make such order as it may think fit for cancelling or varying the registration of a trade mark on the ground of any contravention, or failure to observe a condition entered on the register in relation thereto.

sub_structure.2: (2) Any person aggrieved by an absent, wrongly made, or wrongly remaining entry, or by any error or defect in the register, may apply for rectification.
sub_structure.4: (4) The Registrar or the High Court may, of its own motion, after notice and hearing, make any such rectification order.

plain_english_summary: The general rectification remedy - anyone aggrieved by a wrongful, defective, or condition-breaching trade mark entry can apply to the Registrar or High Court to cancel or correct it; this is the mechanism used to challenge a competitor's improperly obtained registration.

chapter_title: RECTIFICATION AND CORRECTION OF THE REGISTER
title: Correction of register
text: (1) The Registrar may, on application by the registered proprietor, correct any error in the name, address or description of the proprietor or any other register entry, enter any change of name/address/description, cancel a trade mark entry, or strike out goods/classes from a registration, along with any consequential certificate amendment.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Registrar may similarly correct errors or record changes in the name, address or description of a registered user, on application by the registered user and after notice to the proprietor.

plain_english_summary: The administrative mechanism for keeping the register accurate - fixing typos, recording address/name changes, narrowing a registration's goods/services, and similarly updating a licensee's (registered user's) recorded details.

chapter_title: RECTIFICATION AND CORRECTION OF THE REGISTER
title: Alteration of registered trade marks
text: (1) The registered proprietor of a trade mark may apply in the prescribed manner to the Registrar for leave to add to or alter the trade mark in any manner not substantially affecting the identity thereof, and the Registrar may refuse leave or grant it on such terms and subject to such limitations as he may think fit.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Registrar may advertise such an application where expedient, allowing third parties to oppose it.
sub_structure.3: (3) Where leave is granted, the altered trade mark shall be advertised, unless already advertised under sub-section (2).

plain_english_summary: Lets a brand owner make minor tweaks to a registered mark (e.g. small logo refinements) without a fresh application, provided the change doesn't substantially alter the mark's identity - bigger rebrands would instead need a new registration.

chapter_title: RECTIFICATION AND CORRECTION OF THE REGISTER
title: Adaptation of entries in register to amended or substituted classification of goods or services
text: (1) The Registrar shall not amend the register in a way that adds goods/classes/services to an existing registration or antedates a registration, except where the addition/antedating would not affect a substantial quantity of goods/services and would not substantially prejudice any person's rights, in cases involving undue complexity from a changed international classification.

sub_structure.2: (2) A proposed amendment under this section must be notified to the affected registered proprietor and advertised, and may be opposed by any aggrieved person.

plain_english_summary: A housekeeping provision that lets the Registrar update old registrations to match a revised international classification system, without letting owners improperly expand or backdate their registered scope.

title: Special provisions for collective marks
text: (1) The provisions of this Act shall apply to collective marks subject to the provisions contained in this Chapter.

sub_structure.2: (2) In relation to a collective mark, the reference in the definition of 'trade mark' to distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others is read as distinguishing the goods or services of members of an association of persons which is the proprietor of the mark from those of others.

plain_english_summary: Collective marks (owned by an association and used by its members, e.g. an industry body's certification-style badge) are governed by the ordinary trade mark rules as modified by this chapter.

title: Collective mark not to be misleading as to character or significance
text: A collective mark shall not be registered if it is likely to deceive or cause confusion on the part of the public, in particular if it is likely to be taken to be something other than a collective mark, and in such case the Registrar may require that the mark comprise some indication that it is a collective mark.
plain_english_summary: A collective mark must clearly signal that it is a collective mark rather than an ordinary single-owner brand, to avoid misleading consumers.

title: Application to be accompanied by regulations governing use of collective marks
text: (1) An application for registration of a collective mark shall be accompanied by the regulations governing the use of such collective mark.

sub_structure.2: (2) The regulations must specify persons authorised to use the mark, conditions of membership of the association, conditions of use of the mark (including sanctions against misuse), and other prescribed matters.

plain_english_summary: Registering a collective mark requires filing a rulebook up front - who can use it, membership conditions, and sanctions for misuse - analogous to a licensing agreement's governance terms.

title: Acceptance of application and regulations by Registrar
text: If it appears to the Registrar that the requirements for registration are satisfied, he shall accept the application together with the regulations, either unconditionally or subject to conditions/amendments, or refuse to accept it, and if accepted shall notify the regulations.
plain_english_summary: The Registrar reviews and approves (possibly with conditions) both the collective mark application and its governing regulations before registration and publication.

title: Regulations to be open to inspection
text: The regulations referred to in sub-section (1) of section 63 shall be open to public inspection in the same way as the register as provided in section 148.
plain_english_summary: A collective mark's governing regulations are public documents, inspectable the same way as the trade mark register itself.

title: Amendment of regulations
text: Any amendment of regulations referred to in sub-section (1) of section 63 shall not be effective unless the amended regulations are filed with the Registrar, and accepted and published by him in accordance with section 64.
plain_english_summary: Changes to a collective mark's governing rules only take legal effect once filed with, approved by, and published by the Registrar.

title: Infringement proceedings by registered proprietor of collective mark
text: In a suit for infringement instituted by the registered proprietor of a collective mark as plaintiff, the court shall take into account any loss suffered or likely to be suffered by authorised users and may give such directions as it thinks fit as to the extent to which the plaintiff shall hold the proceeds of any pecuniary remedy on behalf of such authorised users.
plain_english_summary: When the owner of a collective mark sues for infringement, the court can factor in the losses suffered by the association's member-users and direct that some of any damages recovered be held on their behalf.

title: Additional grounds for removal of registration of collective mark
text: The registration of a collective mark may also be removed from the register on the ground that the manner in which it has been used has caused it to become liable to mislead the public as a collective mark, or that the proprietor has failed to observe or secure observance of the regulations governing its use.

sub_structure.explanation1: Explanation I.-'authorised user' means a member of an association authorised to use the registered collective mark of the association.
sub_structure.explanation2: Explanation II.-Use of a collective mark by an authorised user is deemed to be use by the registered proprietor.

plain_english_summary: A collective mark can be struck off if it becomes misleading in practice or if the owning association fails to enforce its own usage regulations - mirroring the quality-control rationale behind ordinary trademark licensing.

title: Certain provisions of this Act not applicable to certification trade marks
text: The following provisions of this Act shall not apply to certification trade marks: clauses (a) and (c) of section 9(1); sections 18, 20 and 21 except as expressly applied by this Chapter; sections 28, 29, 30, 41, 42, 47, 48, 49, 50, 52, 54 and section 56(2); and Chapter XII except section 107.
plain_english_summary: Certification trade marks (which certify a standard rather than indicate commercial origin, e.g. an eco-label) are carved out of several ordinary provisions - including the registered-user/licensing sections 48-54 - because Chapter IX supplies its own bespoke regime for them.

title: Registration of certification trade marks
text: A mark shall not be registrable as a certification trade mark in the name of a person who carries on a trade in goods of the kind certified or a trade of the provision of services of the kind certified.
plain_english_summary: The owner of a certification mark cannot itself trade in the certified goods/services - certification must come from an independent, disinterested certifying body.

title: Applications for registration of certification trade marks
text: (1) An application for the registration of a mark as a certification trade mark shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed manner by the person proposed to be registered as the proprietor, accompanied by a draft of the regulations to be deposited under section 74.

sub_structure.2: (2) Sections 18, 19 and 22 apply to such applications (with 'acceptance' read as 'authorisation to proceed').
sub_structure.3: (3) The Registrar or the High Court, as the case may be, must also consider whether the mark would include some indication that it is a certification trade mark.

plain_english_summary: Sets out the certification-mark application process, including filing a draft rulebook (the certification regulations) up front alongside the application.

title: Consideration of application for registration by Registrar
text: (1) The Registrar shall consider whether the applicant is competent to certify the goods, whether the draft regulations to be filed under section 74 are satisfactory, and whether registration would be to the public advantage, and may refuse the application or accept it (with or without modifications/conditions).

sub_structure.2: (2) Except where accepted without modification, the Registrar must give the applicant an opportunity to be heard before deciding.

plain_english_summary: The Registrar vets a certification-mark applicant's competence to certify, the adequacy of the proposed certification rules, and overall public benefit before approving registration.

title: Opposition to registration of certification trade marks
text: When an application has been accepted, the Registrar shall cause the application to be advertised in the prescribed manner, and the provisions of section 21 shall apply in relation to the registration of the mark as they apply to an application under section 18.
plain_english_summary: Accepted certification mark applications go through the same advertisement-and-opposition process (section 21) as an ordinary trade mark application.

title: Filing of regulations governing use of a certification trade mark
text: (1) There shall be filed at the Trade Marks Registry, for every mark registered as a certification trade mark, regulations governing its use - including the cases in which the proprietor is to certify goods/services and authorise use of the mark, and any provisions the Registrar requires or permits (including a right of appeal to the Registrar against a proprietor's refusal to certify goods or to authorise use of the mark) - open to inspection like the register.

sub_structure.2: (2) The filed regulations may, on the registered proprietor's application, be altered by the Registrar.
sub_structure.3: (3) The Registrar may advertise such an alteration application and must hear objectors before deciding.

plain_english_summary: Requires a certification mark's governing rulebook to be publicly filed and lets applicants for use of the mark appeal to the Registrar if the certifying proprietor unfairly refuses to certify them or authorise use.

title: Infringement of certification trade marks
text: The right conferred by section 78 is infringed by any person who, not being the registered proprietor or an authorised person using it in accordance with the filed regulations, uses in the course of trade a mark identical with, or deceptively similar to, the certification trade mark in relation to any goods or services for which it is registered, in a manner likely to be taken as trade mark use.
plain_english_summary: Mirrors ordinary trade mark infringement (section 29) but tailored to certification marks - unauthorised use of an identical or confusingly similar certification mark is infringement.

title: Acts not constituting infringement of certification trade marks
text: (1) It is not infringement to use a certification trade mark within its registered conditions/limitations; to use it on goods/services genuinely certified by, or with the consent of, the proprietor and not subsequently altered; or to use it to indicate goods/services adapted to be accessories to already-certified goods, provided this is reasonably necessary and not misleading.

sub_structure.2: (2) The genuine-certification defence does not apply if the certified use is itself contrary to the filed regulations.
sub_structure.3: (3) Use of one of two or more identical/similar registered certification marks does not infringe the other.

plain_english_summary: Carves out defences for genuine certified use and accessory-compatibility labelling in the certification-mark context, similar in spirit to the general defences in section 30.

title: Cancellation or varying of registration of certification trade marks
text: The Registrar may, on application by any person aggrieved and after giving the proprietor an opportunity to oppose, make such order as he thinks fit for expunging or varying any register entry or the regulations, on the ground that the proprietor is no longer competent to certify, has failed to observe the regulations, it is no longer to the public advantage that the mark remains registered, or the regulations should be varied for the public advantage.
plain_english_summary: Gives an enforcement mechanism against a certification mark owner who stops properly policing its own certification standard - public-advantage grounds can force cancellation or a rewrite of the certification regulations.

title: Rights conferred by registration of certification trade marks
text: (1) Subject to the provisions of sections 34, 35 and 76, the registration of a person as proprietor of a certification trade mark in respect of any goods or services shall, if valid, give to that person the exclusive right to the use of the mark in relation to those goods or services.

sub_structure.2: (2) The exclusive right is subject to any conditions and limitations to which the registration is subject.

plain_english_summary: Grants the certification mark owner exclusive rights over the mark itself (as distinct from the certified goods), subject to the same saving provisions and defences that apply to ordinary marks.

title: Appeals to High Court
text: (1) Any person aggrieved by an order or decision of the Registrar under this Act, or the rules made thereunder, may prefer an appeal to the High Court within three months from the date on which the order or decision sought to be appealed against is communicated to such person.

sub_structure.2: (2) No appeal shall be admitted after expiry of that period, unless the High Court is satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay.
sub_structure.3: (3) An appeal to the High Court shall be in the prescribed form, verified in the prescribed manner, and accompanied by a copy of the order/decision appealed against and the prescribed fee.

plain_english_summary: Sets the route and three-month deadline for appealing a Registrar decision (e.g. a refusal to register, or a registered-user cancellation) - since the Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) was abolished in 2021, such appeals now go directly to the High Court.

title: Bar to appear before Registrar
text: On ceasing to hold the office, the erstwhile Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson or other Members shall not appear before the Registrar.
plain_english_summary: A former Chairperson/Member of the now-abolished Intellectual Property Appellate Board is barred from appearing as an advocate/representative before the Registrar - a post-employment conflict-of-interest restriction, entirely rewritten after the IPAB's 2021 abolition.

title: Procedure for application for rectification, etc., before High Court
text: (1) An application for rectification of the register made to the High Court under section 57 shall be in such form as may be prescribed.

sub_structure.2: (2) A certified copy of every order or judgment of the High Court relating to a registered trade mark under this Act shall be communicated to the Registrar, who shall give effect to it and, when so directed, amend or rectify the register accordingly.

plain_english_summary: Governs the procedural mechanics of filing a rectification application directly with the High Court and ensures the Registrar updates the official register once the High Court rules.

title: Appearance of Registrar in legal proceedings
text: (1) The Registrar shall have the right to appear and be heard in any legal proceedings before the High Court in which the relief sought includes alteration or rectification of the register, or in which a question relating to Trade Marks Registry practice is raised, and in certain appeals from Registrar orders on registration applications.

sub_structure.2: (2) Unless the High Court otherwise directs, the Registrar may, instead of appearing, submit a written statement giving relevant particulars, which shall be evidence in the proceeding.

plain_english_summary: Lets the Registrar participate in (or submit a written statement to) High Court proceedings that touch on the register or Registry practice, ensuring the Registry's institutional perspective is available to the court.

title: Meaning of applying trade marks and trade descriptions
text: (1) A person shall be deemed to apply a trade mark or trade description to goods or services who applies it to the goods themselves or in relation to services; applies it to packaging used for goods sold or intended for sale; encloses goods within packaging already bearing the mark/description; uses it in a manner reasonably likely to suggest the goods/services are designated by it; or uses it in an advertisement, invoice, catalogue or similar commercial document under which goods are delivered or services rendered pursuant to an order referencing that mark.

sub_structure.2: (2) A trade mark or trade description is deemed 'applied' to goods whether woven in, impressed on, or otherwise worked into, or annexed or affixed to, the goods or their packaging.

plain_english_summary: Defines, broadly, what counts as 'applying' a trade mark or trade description to goods or services - the foundational concept for the criminal offences in the rest of this chapter (falsification, false application, and false representation of registration).

title: Falsifying and falsely applying trade marks
text: (1) A person falsifies a trade mark who, without the proprietor's assent, makes that trade mark or a deceptively similar mark, or who falsifies any genuine trade mark by alteration, addition, effacement or otherwise.

sub_structure.2: (2) A person falsely applies a trade mark to goods or services who, without the proprietor's assent, applies the trade mark or a deceptively similar mark to them, or uses packaging bearing an identical/deceptively similar mark to pack goods other than the proprietor's genuine goods.
sub_structure.4: (4) In any prosecution for falsifying or falsely applying a trade mark, the burden of proving the proprietor's assent lies on the accused.

plain_english_summary: Defines the core counterfeiting offences (making a fake mark, or applying someone else's mark to non-genuine goods) that underpin the penal provisions in sections 103-105, and reverses the burden of proof onto the accused to show the proprietor's consent.

title: Penalty for applying false trade marks, trade descriptions, etc.
text: Any person who falsifies any trade mark, falsely applies a trade mark to goods or services, makes or possesses any instrument for falsifying a trade mark, applies a false trade description, applies a false country-of-origin/manufacturer indication where required under section 139, tampers with a required origin indication, or causes any of these to be done, shall - unless he proves he acted without intent to defraud - be punishable with imprisonment for a term of not less than six months (extendable to three years) and a fine of not less than fifty thousand rupees (extendable to two lakh rupees).

sub_structure.proviso: Provided that the court may, for adequate and special reasons recorded in the judgment, impose a lesser sentence of imprisonment or a lesser fine than the statutory minimum.

plain_english_summary: The headline counterfeiting offence - trademark counterfeiting carries a minimum six-month jail term (up to three years) and a minimum fifty-thousand-rupee fine (up to two lakh rupees), with a narrow judicial discretion to go below the minimums for special reasons.

title: Penalty for selling goods or providing services to which false trade mark or false trade description is applied
text: Any person who sells, hires, exposes for sale, or possesses for sale goods or things, or provides or hires services, bearing a false trade mark or false trade description, or lacking a required origin indication under section 139, shall be punishable with the same imprisonment and fine as under section 103, unless he proves he took reasonable precautions and had no reason to suspect the mark/description was false, gave all information he had about his source on demand, or otherwise acted innocently.
plain_english_summary: Extends the same counterfeiting-level penalties to downstream sellers/distributors of counterfeit or falsely-described goods (not just the counterfeiter), with an 'innocent dealer' defence for those who took reasonable precautions and cooperated with the investigation.

title: Enhanced penalty on second or subsequent conviction
