text: Whoever, having already been convicted of an offence under section 103 or 104, is again convicted of any such offence shall be punishable, for the second and every subsequent offence, with imprisonment for a term not less than one year (extendable to three years) and a fine not less than one lakh rupees (extendable to two lakh rupees).

sub_structure.proviso: Provided that the court may, for adequate and special reasons recorded in the judgment, impose a lesser sentence or fine.
sub_structure.proviso2: Provided further that no cognizance shall be taken of any conviction made before the commencement of this Act.

plain_english_summary: Repeat trademark-counterfeiting offenders face steeper mandatory minimums - at least one year's imprisonment and a one-lakh-rupee fine - reflecting the Act's escalating deterrence for recidivist counterfeiters.

title: Penalty for falsely representing a trade mark as registered
text: (1) No person shall represent that an unregistered mark is a registered trade mark, that an unregistered part of a registered mark is separately registered, that a registered trade mark is registered for goods/services for which it is not, or that registration gives an exclusive right broader than the register's actual conditions/limitations allow.

sub_structure.2: (2) Contravention makes the person liable to a penalty equal to one half per cent of total sales/turnover or gross receipts (as per audited accounts), or five lakh rupees, whichever is less.
sub_structure.3: (3) Using the word 'registered' or similar wording/symbols in India in relation to a trade mark is deemed to refer to registration under this Act's register, unless it is clearly linked to a foreign registration under a foreign country's law (e.g. for export-only goods to that country).

plain_english_summary: Bars falsely claiming a mark is registered (the classic misuse of the (R) symbol on an unregistered brand) - the penalty was overhauled in 2023 to be a turnover-linked sum (0.5% of turnover, capped at five lakh rupees) rather than a fixed fine, and applies to Indian claims of registration specifically, carving out clearly-foreign registration claims.

title: No offence in certain cases
text: The provisions of sections 102, 103, 104 and 105 shall, in relation to a registered trade mark or its proprietor, be subject to the rights created or recognised by this Act, and no act or omission shall be deemed an offence under those sections if the alleged offence relates to a registered trade mark and the act/omission is permitted under this Act, or relates to a registered or unregistered trade mark and is permitted under any other law in force.
plain_english_summary: A safe harbour confirming that conduct actually authorised by the Act (or by another law) - for example, use falling within the section 30 defences - cannot itself be prosecuted as a trademark offence.

title: Forfeiture of goods
text: (1) Where a person is convicted (or acquitted on proof of acting without intent to defraud or of the section 104 defences) of an offence under sections 103, 104 or 105, the court may direct the forfeiture to Government of all goods and things by means of, or in relation to, which the offence was committed or would have been committed.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where forfeiture is directed on conviction and an appeal lies against the conviction, an appeal shall also lie against the forfeiture.
sub_structure.3: (3) Where forfeiture is directed on acquittal and the goods exceed fifty rupees in value, an appeal against the forfeiture may be brought within thirty days.
sub_structure.4: (4) On a conviction-based forfeiture, the court may order the forfeited articles destroyed or otherwise disposed of.

plain_english_summary: Lets a criminal court order counterfeit goods (and the tools used to make them) confiscated by the Government - and even permits forfeiture on acquittal in some cases - with a separate appeal right against the forfeiture order itself.

title: Exemption of certain persons employed in ordinary course of business
text: Where a person accused of an offence under section 103 proves he was, in the ordinary course of business, employed on behalf of others to apply trade marks/descriptions or to make instruments for making trade marks; that he was so employed in the case charged and had no profit/commission interest in the goods or services; that, having taken all reasonable precautions, he had no reason to suspect the genuineness of the mark/description; and that he gave all information in his power about the persons on whose behalf he acted on demand, he shall be acquitted.
plain_english_summary: Protects ordinary employees/contractors (e.g. a print shop or packaging vendor) who innocently and unknowingly applied a counterfeit mark on someone else's instructions, provided they cooperate fully with the investigation - relevant to any vendor/agency that a software or hardware company outsources branding/manufacturing work to.

title: Adjudication of penalties
text: The Registrar may, by an order, authorise an officer referred to in section 3, to be adjudicating officer for holding an inquiry and imposing penalty under the provisions of this Act, in the manner as may be prescribed, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard.
plain_english_summary: A 2023-2024 reform inserting an in-house adjudication mechanism: instead of every statutory penalty (such as the section 107 or 140 penalties) needing a full court prosecution, the Registrar can designate an adjudicating officer to hold an inquiry and impose the penalty administratively, after a hearing - part of the broader 'Jan Vishwas' decriminalisation push that converted some trademark offences into civil/administrative penalties.

title: Appeal
text: (1) Whoever is aggrieved by an order of the adjudicating officer under section 112A may prefer an appeal to the appellate authority, who shall be an officer at least one rank above the adjudicating officer, within sixty days from receipt of the order, as the Central Government may by notification authorise.

sub_structure.3: (3) An appeal may be admitted after the sixty-day period if the appellant satisfies the appellate authority there was sufficient cause for the delay.
sub_structure.5: (5) The appellate authority shall dispose of the appeal within sixty days from filing.
sub_structure.6: (6) If a person fails to comply with the adjudicating officer's or appellate authority's order within ninety days, he shall, in addition to the original penalty, be punishable with a fine of one lakh rupees or imprisonment up to one year, or both.

plain_english_summary: Provides an internal appeal route against the new administrative penalty orders under section 112A, with strict sixty-day timelines, and backstops non-compliance with the eventual order by an additional criminal-style fine/imprisonment penalty - companies should route any adjudication-officer penalty notice through this appeal mechanism promptly rather than ignoring it.

title: Procedure where invalidity of registration is pleaded by the accused
text: (1) Where an offence under sections 103, 104 or 105 concerns a registered trade mark and the accused pleads the registration is invalid, and the court finds the defence prima facie tenable, it shall adjourn the case for three months to let the accused apply to the High Court for rectification; if the accused proves such an application was timely filed, the prosecution stays pending the rectification outcome; if no such application is filed in time, the court proceeds as if the registration were valid.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where a rectification application concerning the mark is already pending before the Registrar or High Court when the prosecution complaint is filed, the court shall stay the prosecution pending that application's outcome.

plain_english_summary: Lets a defendant in a counterfeiting prosecution challenge the validity of the plaintiff's trade mark registration, triggering a stay of the criminal case while a proper rectification application is pursued at the High Court, rather than letting the criminal court itself decide validity.

title: Offences by companies
text: (1) If the person committing an offence under this Act is a company, the company and every person in charge of and responsible to it for the conduct of its business at the time of the offence shall be deemed guilty and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly, unless such a person proves the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised all due diligence to prevent it.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where the offence is proved to have been committed with the consent, connivance, or attributable neglect of any director, manager, secretary or other officer, that person is also deemed guilty and liable to be proceeded against.
sub_structure.explanation: Explanation.-'company' includes a firm or other association of individuals; 'director' in relation to a firm means a partner.

plain_english_summary: Standard corporate criminal-liability provision: a company committing a trademark offence exposes both the company and its responsible officers/directors to prosecution, with a due-diligence defence available - directly relevant to founders and executives of a software company accused of trademark-related offences (e.g. via a rogue vendor or reseller's conduct).

title: Cognizance of certain offences and the powers of police officer for search and seizure
text: (1) No court shall take cognizance of an offence under sections 107, 108 or 109 except on a written complaint by the Registrar or an officer authorised by him, though a court shall take cognizance under section 107(1)(c) based on a Registrar's certificate.

sub_structure.2: (2) No court inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class shall try an offence under this Act.
sub_structure.3: (3) Offences under sections 103, 104 and 105 are cognizable.
sub_structure.4: (4) A police officer not below the rank of deputy superintendent may search and seize (without warrant) goods/instruments involved in such an offence, after obtaining and abiding by the Registrar's opinion on the trade mark facts, producing seized articles before a Magistrate as soon as practicable.
sub_structure.5: (5) A person with an interest in seized articles may, within fifteen days, apply to the Magistrate for their return.

plain_english_summary: Gives police real teeth against counterfeiting - warrantless search and seizure powers for the cognizable offences in sections 103-105, subject to first obtaining the Registrar's opinion on the trademark facts - while gating prosecutions under the registration-related offences (section 107 etc.) behind a formal Registrar complaint.

title: Evidence of origin of goods imported by sea
text: In the case of goods brought into India by sea, evidence of the port of shipment shall, in a prosecution under this Act or the relevant Customs Act provisions relating to confiscation of goods for trade mark protection, be prima facie evidence of the place or country in which the goods were made or produced.
plain_english_summary: An evidentiary shortcut in counterfeit-import prosecutions: the port a shipment left from can serve as prima facie proof of the goods' true origin.

title: Costs of defence or prosecution
text: In any prosecution under this Act, the court may order such costs to be paid by the accused to the complainant, or by the complainant to the accused, as the court deems reasonable having regard to the circumstances and conduct of the parties, and the costs so awarded shall be recoverable as if they were a fine.
plain_english_summary: Lets the court shift litigation costs between the parties in a trademark prosecution, and treats an unpaid costs order like an unpaid fine for recovery purposes.

title: Limitation of prosecution
text: No prosecution for an offence under this Act, or under the relevant Customs Act provision for confiscation of goods for trade mark protection, shall be commenced after three years from the commission of the offence, or two years after its discovery by the prosecutor, whichever expires first.
plain_english_summary: Sets a limitation period for launching a trademark-offence prosecution - three years from the offence, or two years from discovery, whichever comes first - so counterfeiting claims cannot be revived indefinitely.

title: Information as to commission of offence
text: An officer of the Government whose duty it is to take part in the enforcement of the provisions of this Chapter shall not be compelled in any court to say whence he got any information as to the commission of any offence against this Act.
plain_english_summary: Protects the confidentiality of informant sources for government enforcement officers investigating trademark offences.

title: Punishment of abetment in India of acts done out of India
text: If any person, being within India, abets the commission, without India, of any act which, if committed in India, would under this Act be an offence, he may be tried for such abetment in any place in India in which he may be found, and be punished with the punishment to which he would be liable if he had himself committed the abetted act in that place.
plain_english_summary: Extends criminal liability to someone in India who helps orchestrate a trademark offence carried out abroad, treating the abetment as if the underlying act had been committed in India - relevant to cross-border counterfeiting or outsourced infringing manufacturing.

title: Instructions of Central Government as to permissible variation to be observed by criminal courts
text: The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, issue instructions for the limits of variation, as regards number, quantity, measure, gauge or weight, which are to be recognised by criminal courts as permissible in the case of any goods.
plain_english_summary: Lets the government set tolerances (e.g. minor measurement variances) that criminal courts should treat as acceptable rather than as a false trade description.

title: Protection of action taken in good faith
text: No suit or other legal proceedings shall lie against any person in respect of anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of this Act.
plain_english_summary: Shields officials and others acting in good faith under the Act (e.g. Registry staff, or a party relying in good faith on a registration) from being sued over their good-faith actions.

title: Certain persons to be public servants
text: Every person appointed under this Act shall be deemed to be a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.
plain_english_summary: Trade Marks Registry officials are legally treated as public servants, exposing them to the Penal Code's protections and liabilities that apply to government officials.

title: Stay of proceedings where the validity of registration of the trade mark is questioned, etc.
text: (1) Where in an infringement suit the defendant pleads the plaintiff's trade mark registration is invalid, or raises the honest-concurrent-use defence under section 30(2)(e) and the plaintiff pleads the defendant's registration is invalid, the trial court shall stay the suit if rectification proceedings on the relevant mark are already pending before the Registrar or High Court, or, if none are pending and the plea is prima facie tenable, frame an issue and adjourn for three months to let the party apply to the High Court for rectification.

sub_structure.2: (2) If the party proves timely filing of the rectification application, the suit's trial stays until that application is finally disposed of.
sub_structure.3: (3) If no such application is filed in time, the invalidity issue is deemed abandoned and the suit proceeds on the other issues.
sub_structure.5: (5) The stay does not prevent the court from making interlocutory orders (injunctions, accounts, receivers, attachment) during the stay period.

plain_english_summary: When a trademark infringement lawsuit turns on whether the plaintiff's (or defendant's) registration is actually valid, that validity question must go to the High Court via a rectification application rather than being decided by the trial court itself - though the trial court can still grant interim relief like injunctions while that plays out.

title: Application for rectification of register to be made to High Court in certain cases
text: (1) Where in an infringement suit the validity of the plaintiff's or defendant's trade mark registration is questioned (including via the section 30(2)(e) defence), the validity issue shall be determined only on an application for rectification made to the High Court, not the Registrar, notwithstanding sections 47 or 57.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where a rectification application on the same point is already pending before the Registrar under section 47 or 57, the Registrar may, if he thinks fit, refer it to the High Court at any stage.

plain_english_summary: Once trademark validity becomes a live issue inside an infringement suit, the rectification application must be routed to the High Court (not filed separately with the Registrar), keeping validity and infringement questions before the same forum.

title: Implied warranty on sale of marked goods
text: Where a mark or trade description has been applied to goods on sale, or in a contract of sale, or in relation to a service, the seller is deemed to warrant that the mark is genuine and not falsely applied, or that the trade description is not false, unless the contrary is expressed in writing and delivered at the time of sale and accepted by the buyer.
plain_english_summary: Selling branded/described goods automatically carries an implied warranty that the mark and description are genuine, unless the seller expressly and in writing disclaims that at the point of sale - relevant to any reseller or marketplace selling branded software/hardware products.

title: Powers of Registrar
text: In all proceedings under this Act before the Registrar, the Registrar has all the powers of a civil court for receiving evidence, administering oaths, enforcing witness attendance, and compelling document production and discovery; may make cost orders (executable as a civil court decree) subject to rules, except in appeals against a certification-mark proprietor's refusal to certify; and may, on application, review his own decisions.
plain_english_summary: Equips the Registrar with civil-court-like powers (evidence-taking, discovery, cost orders, self-review of decisions) for conducting Trade Marks Registry proceedings such as oppositions and rectifications.

title: Exercise of discretionary power by Registrar
text: Subject to the provisions of section 131, the Registrar shall not exercise any discretionary or other power vested in him by this Act or the rules adversely to a person applying for the exercise of that power without (if requested within the prescribed time) giving that person an opportunity of being heard.
plain_english_summary: Basic natural-justice safeguard: before ruling against an applicant on a discretionary matter, the Registrar must give them a chance to be heard if they ask for one in time.

title: Evidence before Registrar
text: In any proceeding under this Act before the Registrar, evidence shall be given by affidavit, provided that the Registrar may, if he thinks fit, take oral evidence in lieu of, or in addition to, such evidence by affidavit.
plain_english_summary: Registry proceedings normally run on affidavit evidence, with the Registrar retaining discretion to hear oral evidence as well or instead.

title: Death of party to a proceeding
text: If a person who is a party to a proceeding under this Act (not being a proceeding before a court) dies pending the proceeding, the Registrar may, on request and proof of transmission of the deceased's interest, substitute the successor in interest in his place, or, if satisfied the surviving parties sufficiently represent the deceased's interest, permit the proceeding to continue without such substitution.
plain_english_summary: Lets a Registry proceeding continue smoothly if a party dies mid-way, by substituting their legal successor or proceeding without formal substitution if the interest is otherwise represented.

title: Extension of time
text: (1) If the Registrar is satisfied, on a prescribed application and fee, that there is sufficient cause for extending the time for doing any act (not being a time expressly fixed by the Act itself), he may, subject to such conditions as he thinks fit, extend the time and inform the parties.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Registrar need not hear the parties before deciding such an extension application, and no appeal lies from his order under this section.

plain_english_summary: Gives the Registrar general discretion to grant deadline extensions for procedural steps (other than statutory deadlines fixed directly by the Act), with the decision being final and non-appealable.

title: Abandonment
text: Where, in the Registrar's opinion, an applicant is in default in prosecuting an application filed under this Act (or a prior trade marks law), the Registrar may, by notice, require the applicant to remedy the default within a specified time and, after an opportunity of hearing if desired, treat the application as abandoned unless the default is remedied in time.
plain_english_summary: An applicant who lets an application go stale (missing required steps or Registry deadlines) risks having it treated as abandoned after notice and a chance to fix the default.

title: Preliminary advice by the Registrar as to distinctiveness
text: (1) The Registrar may, on application by a prospective applicant, give advice as to whether a proposed trade mark appears to him prima facie to be distinctive.

sub_structure.2: (2) If a subsequent registration application (filed within three months of favourable advice) is later objected to on distinctiveness grounds, the applicant can withdraw and get a refund of the filing fee.

plain_english_summary: Lets a business get an informal, non-binding preliminary read from the Registrar on whether a candidate brand name/logo looks distinctive enough to register - useful due diligence before committing to a name, with a fee-refund safety net if the Registrar later changes course.

title: Suit for infringement, etc., to be instituted before District Court
text: (1) No suit for infringement of a registered trade mark, relating to any right in a registered trade mark, or for passing off arising from use of an identical or deceptively similar mark (whether registered or unregistered), shall be instituted in any court inferior to a District Court having jurisdiction to try the suit.

sub_structure.2: (2) 'District Court having jurisdiction' includes, notwithstanding the CPC, a District Court within whose jurisdiction the person instituting the suit (plaintiff) actually and voluntarily resides, carries on business, or personally works for gain - a plaintiff-friendly jurisdiction rule.
sub_structure.explanation: Explanation.-For sub-section (2), 'person' includes the registered proprietor and the registered user.

plain_english_summary: Sets the minimum court level (District Court) for trademark infringement/passing-off suits, and - notably - lets the plaintiff (including a registered user/licensee) sue in the courts local to where they themselves are based, rather than only where the defendant is, making it easier for a brand owner or its licensee to enforce rights close to home.

title: Relief in suits for infringement or for passing off
text: (1) The relief a court may grant in an infringement or passing-off suit includes injunction (on such terms as the court thinks fit) and, at the plaintiff's option, either damages or an account of profits, with or without an order for delivery-up of infringing labels and marks for destruction or erasure.

sub_structure.2: (2) The injunction may include ex parte or interlocutory orders for discovery of documents, preserving infringing goods/evidence, or restraining the defendant from dealing with assets in a way that would prejudice recovery of damages.
sub_structure.3: (3) The court shall not award damages (other than nominal damages) or an account of profits where the infringement involves a certification/collective mark, or where the defendant proves innocent adoption and prompt cessation of use on becoming aware of the plaintiff's rights (an 'innocent infringer' defence, applicable both to registered-mark infringement and passing off).

plain_english_summary: Defines the remedies available in trademark litigation - injunctions, damages or an account of profits, and destruction of infringing material - plus an important 'innocent infringer' carve-out that can spare a defendant from monetary liability (though not necessarily an injunction) if they genuinely didn't know about the conflicting mark and stopped promptly once they learned of it.

title: Registered user to be impleaded in certain proceedings
text: (1) In every proceeding under Chapter VII (rectification) or under section 91 (appeals), every registered user of the trade mark by way of permitted use who is not himself an applicant in that proceeding shall be made a party to it.

sub_structure.2: (2) A registered user so made a party shall not be liable for any costs unless he enters an appearance and takes part in the proceeding.

plain_english_summary: A recorded trademark licensee (registered user) must be joined as a party to rectification or appeal proceedings affecting the mark it licenses, but only bears cost risk if it actively participates - protecting licensees' interests without forcing them to litigate.

title: Evidence of entries in register, etc., and things done by the Registrar
text: (1) A copy of any register entry or of any document under section 148(1), certified by the Registrar and sealed with the Trade Marks Registry seal, shall be admitted in evidence in all courts and proceedings without further proof or production of the original.

sub_structure.2: (2) A certificate under the Registrar's hand as to any entry, matter or thing he is authorised to make or do shall be prima facie evidence of that entry, its contents, or that the matter/thing was done or not done.

plain_english_summary: Makes certified Registry documents self-proving in court - no need to call the Registrar as a witness or produce the original register to prove a registration's contents.

title: Registrar and other officers not compellable to produce register, etc.
text: The Registrar or any officer of the Trade Marks Registry shall not, in legal proceedings to which he is not a party, be compellable to produce the register or any document in his custody (whose contents can be proved by a certified copy) or to appear as a witness, unless the court orders it for special cause.
plain_english_summary: Shields Registry officials from routine subpoenas in litigation they aren't party to, since certified copies already serve as proof - unless a court finds special cause to compel them.

title: Power to require goods to show indication of origin
text: (1) The Central Government may, by notification, require that goods of a specified class (whether imported or domestically made) bear, from a date not less than three months after the notification, an indication of their country/place of origin or the name and address of the manufacturer.

sub_structure.3: (3) No such notification shall issue unless applied for by persons/associations substantially representing the affected trade interests, or unless the Central Government is otherwise convinced it is necessary in the public interest.
sub_structure.5: (5) The notification does not apply to imported goods that Customs is satisfied are intended purely for re-export.

plain_english_summary: Empowers the government to mandate country-of-origin/manufacturer labelling for specified categories of goods - a precursor requirement to the false-origin-indication offences in sections 103/104.

title: Power to require information of imported goods bearing false trade marks
text: (1) The proprietor or licensee of a registered trade mark may give notice in writing to the Collector of Customs to prohibit importation of goods whose import would infringe under section 29(6)(c).

sub_structure.2: (2) Where goods prohibited under the Customs Act for trade mark protection are imported, the Commissioner of Customs, on representation and reasonable belief that a false trade mark is used, may require the importer or agent to produce documents and furnish consignor/consignee information.
sub_structure.3: (3) The importer or agent must comply within fourteen days, failing which he is liable to a penalty of ten thousand rupees, levied and recovered by the Customs Act authority.

plain_english_summary: Lets a trade mark owner (or its licensee) trigger a Customs-border enforcement mechanism against suspected counterfeit imports; the 2023-2024 reform replaced the old criminal-style sanction for non-cooperating importers with a fixed ten-thousand-rupee administrative penalty recoverable under the Customs Act - relevant to a software/hardware company worried about counterfeit devices or media entering India.

title: Certificate of validity
text: If in any legal proceeding for rectification of the register before the High Court a decision is on contest given in favour of the registered proprietor on the issue of the registration's validity, the High Court may grant a certificate to that effect; and in any subsequent proceeding where that validity again comes into question, the proprietor, on obtaining a final order/judgment affirming validity, shall (unless the order directs otherwise for sufficient reason) be entitled to full costs, charges and expenses as between legal practitioner and client.
plain_english_summary: Rewards a trade mark owner who successfully defends their registration's validity once with a 'certificate of validity' that entitles them to enhanced (full solicitor-client) costs if the same validity challenge is raised again later - discouraging repeat vexatious attacks on a settled registration.

title: Groundless threats of legal proceedings
text: (1) Where a person, by circulars, advertisements or otherwise, threatens another with an infringement action or similar proceeding over a trade mark that is registered (or alleged to be registered), a person aggrieved may bring a suit against the threatening party for a declaration that the threats are unjustifiable, an injunction against their continuance, and any damages sustained - unless the threatening party satisfies the court that the trade mark is registered and that the threatened acts do or would constitute infringement.

sub_structure.2: (2) This remedy does not apply if the registered proprietor or a registered user, acting with due diligence, commences and prosecutes an actual infringement action against the threatened person.
sub_structure.3: (3) A legal practitioner or registered trade marks agent acting in a professional capacity on behalf of a client is not personally liable under this section.
sub_structure.4: (4) A suit under this section shall not be instituted in any court inferior to a District Court.

plain_english_summary: Protects businesses from bullying cease-and-desist letters over trade marks: if someone threatens an infringement suit without actually filing one (and without a valid basis), the threatened party can sue for a declaration, an injunction, and damages - a safeguard every software company should know both when sending and when receiving a trademark demand letter, since an over-aggressive cease-and-desist can itself become a liability.

title: Address for service
text: An address for service stated in an application or notice of opposition shall be deemed to be the address of the applicant or opponent for that application/notice, and documents may be served by leaving them at, or posting them to, that address.
plain_english_summary: Establishes that the address given in a Registry filing is the official service address for that proceeding - a housekeeping rule with real consequences if a party fails to keep it updated.

title: Trade usages, etc., to be taken into consideration
text: In any proceeding relating to a trade mark, the Registrar or the High Court, as the case may be, shall admit evidence of the usages of the trade concerned and of any relevant trade mark or trade name or get-up legitimately used by other persons.
plain_english_summary: Requires the Registrar/High Court to consider real-world trade usage and third-party marks/get-up when deciding trademark disputes, rather than assessing marks in a vacuum.

title: Agents
text: Where any act (other than making an affidavit) is required to be done before the Registrar by any person, it may, subject to the rules, be done instead by a duly authorised legal practitioner, a person registered as a trade marks agent, or a person in the sole and regular employment of the principal.
plain_english_summary: Confirms who can act on a client's behalf before the Trade Marks Registry - lawyers, registered trade marks agents, or in-house staff - a practical point for any startup outsourcing its trademark filings and prosecution.

title: Marks registered by an agent or representative without authority
text: If an agent or representative of a registered trade mark's proprietor, without authority, uses, attempts to register, or registers the mark in his own name, the proprietor may oppose the registration, or secure its cancellation or rectification to bring himself onto the register as proprietor by assignment, provided such action is taken within three years of becoming aware of the agent's/representative's conduct.
plain_english_summary: Protects a brand owner against a rogue distributor, local agent, or reseller who tries to register the owner's mark in its own name without permission - a real risk when a software or hardware company appoints local resellers/distributors abroad or in India without properly documenting who owns the brand, and gives a three-year window from discovery to act.

title: Indexes
text: There shall be kept under the direction and supervision of the Registrar an index of registered trade marks, an index of trade marks in respect of which applications are pending, an index of the names of proprietors of registered trade marks, and an index of the names of registered users.
plain_english_summary: Requires the Registry to maintain searchable indexes - including of registered users (licensees) - useful for due diligence when checking who owns or has licensed a given brand.

title: Documents open to public inspection
text: (1) Save as otherwise provided in section 49(4), the register and its underlying documents, notices of opposition and rectification applications with counter-statements and affidavits, regulations deposited under sections 63/74 and applications to vary them, the indexes under section 147, and other Central Government-specified documents shall, subject to prescribed conditions, be open to public inspection at the Trade Marks Registry.

sub_structure.2: (2) Any person may, on application and payment of the prescribed fee, obtain a certified copy of any register entry or document referred to in sub-section (1).

plain_english_summary: Makes most Registry records - including opposition files and collective/certification mark regulations - open for public inspection and certified copies, subject to the section 49(4) carve-out that lets confidential licensing-agreement details be withheld from competitors.

title: Reports of Registrar to be placed before Parliament
text: The Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament once a year a report respecting the execution by or under the Registrar of this Act.
plain_english_summary: Requires an annual report on the Trade Marks Registry's functioning to be tabled in Parliament, as a transparency/accountability mechanism.

title: Fees and surcharge
text: (1) There shall be paid in respect of applications, international applications, registration and other matters under this Act such fees and surcharge as may be prescribed by the Central Government.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where a fee is payable for an act by the Registrar, the Registrar shall not do that act until the fee is paid.
sub_structure.3: (3) Where a fee is payable for filing a document, the document is deemed not filed until the fee is paid.

plain_english_summary: Confirms that all Registry fees (filing, renewal, opposition, registered-user recordal, etc.) are a precondition to the Registrar acting - an unpaid fee means the underlying filing legally hasn't happened yet.

title: Savings in respect of certain matters in Chapter XII
text: Nothing in Chapter XII shall exempt any person from any suit or proceeding that could otherwise be brought against him; entitle any person to refuse complete discovery or to refuse to answer a question in any suit (though such discovery/answer is not admissible against him in a Chapter XII prosecution or related Customs Act confiscation proceeding); or excuse a servant of an India-resident master who, acting in good faith on the master's instructions, gives full information about the master and those instructions on demand.
plain_english_summary: Clarifies that the criminal offences chapter doesn't override ordinary civil remedies or discovery obligations, and gives a limited immunity to an employee who cooperates fully and was simply following a resident employer's instructions in good faith.

title: Declaration as to ownership of trade mark not registrable under the Registration Act, 1908
text: Notwithstanding anything contained in the Registration Act, 1908, no document declaring or purporting to declare the ownership or title of a person to a trade mark other than a registered trade mark shall be registered under that Act.
plain_english_summary: Blocks using the general Registration Act, 1908 as a backdoor way to formally record ownership claims over unregistered trade marks - ownership of a trade mark as such can only be recorded through the Trade Marks Act's own register.

title: Government to be bound
text: The provisions of this Act shall be binding on the Government.
plain_english_summary: The government itself is subject to the Trade Marks Act, including when it owns or uses trade marks.

title: Special provisions relating to applications for registration from citizens of convention countries
text: (1) With a view to the fulfilment of a treaty, convention or arrangement with any country or group/union of countries or Inter-Governmental Organisation outside India which affords to citizens of India similar privileges as granted to its own citizens, the Central Government may, by notification, declare such country, group, union or organisation to be a convention country for the purposes of this Act.

sub_structure.2: (2) A person who applied for registration of a trade mark in a convention country and applies for registration of the same mark in India within six months of that foreign filing gets the benefit of the earlier foreign filing date as the Indian application/registration date (a Paris Convention-style priority claim).
sub_structure.4: (4) This does not entitle recovery of damages for infringement occurring before the actual Indian filing date.

plain_english_summary: Implements the Paris Convention-style priority right: a foreign trade mark application in a reciprocating 'convention country' can be used as the basis for an Indian filing within six months, with the Indian registration backdated to the earlier foreign filing date - important for a software company that first files its brand abroad and wants to preserve priority when filing in India.

title: Provision as to reciprocity
text: Where a specified country or Inter-Governmental Organisation does not accord Indian citizens the same trade mark registration and protection rights it accords its own nationals, no national of that country shall be entitled, solely or jointly, to apply for or be registered as proprietor of a trade mark, to be registered as assignee of a registered trade mark's proprietor, or to apply for or be registered as a registered user of a trade mark.
plain_english_summary: A reciprocity/retaliation provision that can bar nationals of a non-reciprocating country from registering, being assigned, or being licensed (as registered user) Indian trade marks.

title: Power of Central Government to remove difficulties
text: (1) If any difficulty arises in giving effect to the provisions of this Act, the Central Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette, make provisions not inconsistent with the Act as necessary to remove the difficulty, provided no such order is made after five years from the Act's commencement.

sub_structure.2: (2) Every such order shall be laid before each House of Parliament as soon as may be after it is made.

plain_english_summary: A time-limited (five-year) transitional power letting the government patch over implementation gaps by executive order, subject to Parliamentary oversight.

title: Power to make rules
text: (1) The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette and subject to the condition of previous publication, make rules to carry out the provisions of this Act.

sub_structure.2_examples: (2) Without prejudice to that general power, rules may prescribe (among many other matters) how the Register is maintained (s.6); how registration applications, oppositions, corrections and renewals are filed (ss.18-25); the Madrid Protocol international-application process (ss.36D-36E); how assignments/transmissions are recorded (s.45); how registered-user applications, variations and cancellations are made (ss.49-50); rectification application procedure (s.57); and the manner of holding inquiries and imposing penalties under the adjudicating-officer regime (s.112A) and appeals from it (s.112B).
sub_structure.4: (4) Every rule must be laid before both Houses of Parliament for thirty days, during which either House may modify or annul it, without prejudice to anything previously done under the rule.

plain_english_summary: The Act's omnibus rule-making power, delegating the fine-grained procedural detail (forms, fees, timelines) for essentially every Registry process - including trademark licensing (registered-user) procedure and the newer administrative-penalty regime - to Central Government rules, subject to a public-comment requirement and Parliamentary oversight.

title: Amendments
text: The enactment specified in the Schedule shall be amended in the manner specified therein.
plain_english_summary: A short provision giving effect to consequential amendments (set out in the Schedule) to other legislation, such as the Companies Act, 1956, to prevent company names clashing with registered trade marks.

title: Repeal and savings
text: (1) The Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 is hereby repealed.

sub_structure.2: (2) Notifications, rules, orders, registrations, certificates and other things made or done under the 1958 Act that were in force at this Act's commencement continue in force as if made under the corresponding provisions of this Act.
sub_structure.3: (3) This Act applies to any registration application pending at commencement, and to proceedings and registrations consequent on it.
sub_structure.6: (6) The expiration date of a trade mark registered before this Act's commencement is fixed as immediately after seven years from its registration/renewal, with a special five-year sunset for old 'defensive' trade marks under the repealed Act.

plain_english_summary: Repeals the earlier Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 while carrying forward existing registrations, rules and pending matters so that brand owners with pre-existing (1958-era) registrations didn't lose their rights in the transition to the new regime.

title: Short title, extent and commencement
text: (1) This Act may be called the Patents Act, 1970. (2) It extends to the whole of India. (3) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint.

sub_structure.proviso: Different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Act, and any reference in a provision to the commencement of this Act is to be construed as a reference to the coming into force of that provision.

plain_english_summary: The short title, territorial extent (all of India) and staggered commencement clause of the Act — different sections came into force on different notified dates.

title: Definitions and interpretation
text: In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires— (a) "Appellate Board" means the Appellate Board referred to in section 116; (ab) "assignee" includes an assignee of the assignee and the legal representative of a deceased assignee; (ac) "capable of industrial application", in relation to an invention, means that the invention is capable of being made or used in an industry; (b) "Controller" means the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks referred to in section 73.

sub_structure.f: (f) "exclusive licence" means a licence from a patentee which confers on the licensee, to the exclusion of all other persons (including the patentee), any right in respect of the patented invention.
sub_structure.j: (j) "invention" means a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application.
sub_structure.ja: (ja) "inventive step" means a feature of an invention that involves technical advance as compared to existing knowledge or has economic significance (or both) and that makes the invention not obvious to a person skilled in the art.
sub_structure.l: (l) "new invention" means an invention or technology not anticipated by publication or prior use anywhere before the filing date of the complete specification — i.e. not in the public domain and not part of the state of the art.
sub_structure.m: (m) "patent" means a patent for any invention granted under this Act.
sub_structure.p: (p) "patentee" means the person for the time being entered on the register as the grantee or proprietor of the patent.
sub_structure.t: (t) "person interested" includes a person engaged in, or promoting, research in the same field as the invention.
sub_structure.w: (w) "priority date" has the meaning assigned to it by section 11.
sub_structure.y: (y) "true and first inventor" does not include either the first importer of an invention into India, or a person to whom an invention is first communicated from outside India.

plain_english_summary: The Act's core vocabulary. For a software/deep-tech startup the key terms are 'invention' (must be a new product/process with an inventive step and industrial applicability), 'inventive step' (technical advance or economic significance making it non-obvious), 'exclusive licence' (the statutory basis for exclusive patent licensing arrangements), and 'true and first inventor' (relevant to employee/founder inventorship and assignment chains).

title: What are not inventions
text: The following are not inventions within the meaning of this Act— (a) an invention which is frivolous or which claims anything obviously contrary to well established natural laws; (b) an invention the primary or intended use or commercial exploitation of which could be contrary to public order or morality or which causes serious prejudice to human, animal or plant life or health or to the environment; (c) the mere discovery of a scientific principle or the formulation of an abstract theory or discovery of any living thing or non-living substance occurring in nature; (d) the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance which does not result in enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance, or the mere discovery of a new property or new use of a known substance, or the mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus unless it results in a new product or employs at least one new reactant.

sub_structure.d_explanation: Explanation to (d): salts, esters, ethers, polymorphs, metabolites, pure form, particle size, isomers, mixtures of isomers, complexes, combinations and other derivatives of a known substance are considered the same substance unless they differ significantly in properties regarding efficacy (this is India's anti-evergreening rule for pharma patents).
sub_structure.h: (h) a method of agriculture or horticulture.
sub_structure.i: (i) any process for the medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic, diagnostic, therapeutic or other treatment of human beings, or a similar treatment of animals, to render them free of disease or increase their economic value.
sub_structure.j: (j) plants and animals in whole or any part thereof other than micro-organisms, but including seeds, varieties, species, and essentially biological processes for production or propagation of plants and animals.
sub_structure.k: (k) a mathematical or business method or a computer programme per se or algorithms.
sub_structure.l: (l) a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work or any other aesthetic creation whatsoever, including cinematographic works and television productions.
sub_structure.m: (m) a mere scheme or rule or method of performing a mental act or method of playing a game.
sub_structure.p: (p) an invention which, in effect, is traditional knowledge or is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of a traditionally known component or components.

plain_english_summary: The single most important provision in Indian law for software patentability. Clause (k) excludes 'a mathematical or business method or a computer programme per se or algorithms' from patentability — the phrase 'per se' is doing the critical work: it is source code / an abstract algorithm in isolation that cannot be patented, not every invention that happens to involve software. In practice and under Patent Office guidelines, a software-related invention CAN be patented if it produces a further technical effect or is claimed in conjunction with novel hardware/a technical system (e.g. an embedded control system, a networking protocol improvement, a signal-processing method) rather than as a bare algorithm or business method. Clause (m) (mental acts/business methods) and clause (n) (mere presentation of information) are the other clauses most often invoked to reject pure software/SaaS claims, so patent strategy for an Indian software company should frame claims around the technical problem solved and hardware/system integration, not the algorithm alone.

title: Inventions relating to atomic energy not patentable
text: No patent shall be granted in respect of an invention relating to atomic energy falling within sub-section (1) of section 20 of the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 (33 of 1962).
plain_english_summary: A blanket bar on patenting atomic-energy inventions covered by the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 — a narrow sector-specific exclusion, not relevant to most software/IP-licensing work.

title: Persons entitled to apply for patents
text: (1) Subject to the provisions contained in section 134, an application for a patent for an invention may be made by any of the following persons: (a) any person claiming to be the true and first inventor of the invention; (b) any person being the assignee of the person claiming to be the true and first inventor in respect of the right to make such an application; (c) the legal representative of any deceased person who immediately before his death was entitled to make such an application.

sub_structure.2: (2) An application under sub-section (1) may be made by any of the persons referred to therein either alone or jointly with any other person.

plain_english_summary: Defines who can file a patent application in India: the true and first inventor, their assignee (e.g. the startup a founder-inventor has assigned rights to), or a deceased inventor's legal representative — the foundational provision for structuring inventor-to-company assignment chains before filing.

title: Form of application
text: (1) Every application for a patent shall be for one invention only and shall be made in the prescribed form and filed in the patent office. (1A) Every international application under the Patent Cooperation Treaty designating India shall be deemed to be an application under this Act, if a corresponding application has also been filed before the Controller in India.

sub_structure.1B: (1B) The filing date of such an application and its complete specification, processed as designated/elected office, shall be the international filing date accorded under the PCT.
sub_structure.2: (2) Where the application is made by virtue of an assignment of the right to apply, proof of the right to make the application must be furnished with, or shortly after, the application.
sub_structure.3: (3) The application must state that the applicant possesses the invention and name the true and first inventor; if the applicant is not that person, a declaration that the applicant believes the named person to be the true and first inventor is required.
sub_structure.4: (4) Every such application (other than a convention or PCT application) must be accompanied by a provisional or complete specification.

plain_english_summary: Sets the mechanics for filing: one invention per application, prescribed form, PCT national-phase filings in India deemed applications under this Act with the international filing date carried over, and mandatory inventorship declarations — directly relevant to how a startup structures its own patent filing pipeline (including PCT national phase entry).

title: Information and undertaking regarding foreign applications
text: (1) Where an applicant is prosecuting, alone or jointly, a corresponding patent application in a country outside India for the same or substantially the same invention, the applicant must file (a) a statement of detailed particulars of such foreign application, and (b) an undertaking to keep the Controller informed in writing of further particulars of such foreign applications, up to the date of grant in India.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller may also, at any time before grant or refusal, require the applicant to furnish prescribed details of the processing of corresponding foreign applications.

plain_english_summary: A mandatory foreign-filing disclosure duty: an applicant prosecuting a corresponding application abroad must proactively keep the Indian Patent Office updated — failure to comply is itself a ground for opposition/revocation under sections 25 and 64, so this is a standing compliance obligation throughout prosecution, not a one-time filing task.

title: Provisional and complete specifications
text: (1) Where an application (not a convention or PCT application) is accompanied by a provisional specification, a complete specification must be filed within twelve months from the date of filing, failing which the application is deemed abandoned.

sub_structure.2: (2) Two or more applications by the same applicant for cognate inventions may, with the Controller's leave, be combined into a single complete specification, with the 12-month period reckoned from the earliest provisional specification.
sub_structure.3: (3) The Controller may, on request within twelve months, direct that a specification purporting to be complete be treated as provisional instead.
sub_structure.4: (4) The applicant may request cancellation of a provisional specification and post-dating of the application to the date of filing of the complete specification.

plain_english_summary: Governs the classic 'provisional-to-complete' patent filing pathway used by most startups: file a provisional specification to lock in a priority date cheaply, then convert to a complete specification within 12 months or the application lapses — a hard deadline a startup's patent counsel must calendar.

title: Contents of specifications
text: (1) Every specification, provisional or complete, shall describe the invention and begin with a title sufficiently indicating its subject-matter. (2) Drawings may, and if the Controller requires shall, be supplied and are deemed part of the specification.

sub_structure.4: (4) A complete specification must: (a) fully and particularly describe the invention, its operation/use and the method of performing it; (b) disclose the best method known to the applicant; (c) end with a claim or claims defining the scope of protection; (d) be accompanied by an abstract. A proviso sets out biological-material deposit requirements under the Budapest Treaty (deposit before the Indian filing date, full characteristics disclosed, access only after filing/priority date, and disclosure of source/geographical origin).
sub_structure.5: (5) Claims must relate to a single invention or a single inventive concept, be clear, succinct, and fairly based on the specification's disclosure.
sub_structure.6: (6) A declaration as to inventorship must be furnished with, or shortly after, the complete specification.

plain_english_summary: Sets the drafting requirements for a valid specification: full enabling disclosure, best-method disclosure, clear claims, an abstract, and (for biotech/software-adjacent inventions using biological material) Budapest Treaty deposit rules — the technical drafting standard a startup's patent attorney must meet to avoid later insufficiency-of-disclosure attacks under section 64(h).

title: Priority dates of claims of a complete specification
text: (1) There shall be a priority date for each claim of a complete specification. (2) Where a complete specification follows a provisional specification and the claim is fairly based on matter disclosed there, the priority date of that claim is the date of filing of the provisional specification.

sub_structure.3A: (3A) Where a complete specification is based on a previously filed Indian application, filed within twelve months, and fairly based on that application's disclosure, the priority date is the date of the earlier Indian application.
sub_structure.5: (5) Where a claim would otherwise have two or more priority dates, the earliest applies.
sub_structure.8: (8) A claim is not invalid merely because of publication/use of the invention on or after its priority date, or because of the grant of another patent claiming the same invention with the same or a later priority date.

plain_english_summary: Establishes how the crucial 'priority date' of each claim is fixed — the reference date against which novelty and inventive step are judged — including rules for successive Indian filings and multiple provisional-to-complete conversions, which matters for a startup filing a sequence of provisionals as its product evolves.

title: Publication of applications
text: (1) Save as otherwise provided, no application for a patent shall ordinarily be open to the public for such period as may be prescribed (18 months from priority date under the Patent Rules). (2) The applicant may request early publication before expiry of that period, and the Controller shall publish as soon as possible.

sub_structure.3: (3) Every application is published on expiry of the prescribed period except where a secrecy direction under section 35 applies, the application is deemed abandoned under section 9(1), or it was withdrawn at least three months before the publication deadline.
sub_structure.6: (6) On publication, the depository institution must make deposited biological material available to the public, and the patent office may (on fee) make the specification and drawings available.
sub_structure.7: (7) From publication until grant, the applicant has the same privileges/rights as if the patent had already been granted, EXCEPT that no infringement suit can be instituted until the patent is actually granted (rights only crystallize retrospectively on grant).

plain_english_summary: Sets India's default 18-month publication timeline (with an option to request early publication) and, critically, creates a period of provisional/pending patent rights from publication to grant — the applicant can rely on the published claims against would-be infringers once the patent is later granted, but cannot sue until grant actually happens. Important for startups timing enforcement strategy around a pending application.

title: Request for examination
text: (1) No application for a patent shall be examined unless the applicant or any other interested person makes a request for examination, in the prescribed manner, within the prescribed period (48 months from priority date under the Patent Rules).

sub_structure.4: (4) If no request for examination is made within the prescribed period, the application is treated as withdrawn, subject to a proviso allowing the applicant to voluntarily withdraw earlier, and allowing the examination-request window to run from revocation of a secrecy direction under section 35 where applicable.

plain_english_summary: Examination in India is not automatic — the applicant (or even a third party 'other interested person') must affirmatively file a Request for Examination within the prescribed window, or the application is deemed withdrawn. This is a critical, easily-missed deadline for startups managing their own patent portfolios.

title: Examination of application
text: (1) When a request for examination has been made, the application, specification and related documents shall be referred by the Controller to an examiner to report on: (a) compliance with the Act and rules; (b) any lawful ground of objection to grant; (c) the results of the anticipation search under section 13; and (d) any other prescribed matter.

sub_structure.2: (2) The examiner shall ordinarily report to the Controller within the prescribed period.

plain_english_summary: Sets up the substantive examination process: once an RFE is filed, an examiner conducts formal, patentability and prior-art review and reports back to the Controller.

title: Search for anticipation by previous publication and by prior claim
text: (1) The examiner shall investigate whether the claimed invention has been anticipated by publication in an earlier Indian patent application (filed on or after 1 January 1912), or is claimed in another complete specification with an earlier priority date. (2) The examiner shall also search for anticipation by publication in India or elsewhere in any other document (the general prior-art/novelty search).

sub_structure.4: (4) Examination and investigation under sections 12-13 do not warrant the validity of any patent, and no liability attaches to the Government for any examination, investigation, report, or related proceeding.

plain_english_summary: The statutory basis for the Patent Office's prior-art/novelty search (both against earlier Indian filings and the broader world prior art) — importantly, a granted patent's validity is never 'guaranteed' by having passed this search, so downstream invalidity challenges remain available.

title: Consideration of the report of examiner by Controller
text: Where the examiner's report is adverse to the applicant or requires amendment to ensure compliance with the Act or rules, the Controller shall communicate the gist of the objections to the applicant as expeditiously as possible and, if the applicant requires, give an opportunity of being heard.
plain_english_summary: Requires the Controller to share examination objections with the applicant and grant a hearing on request — the procedural backbone of prosecution/office-action practice before the Indian Patent Office.

title: Power of Controller to refuse or require amended applications, etc., in certain cases
text: Where the Controller is satisfied that the application, specification or any related document does not comply with the Act or rules, the Controller may refuse the application, or require it to be amended to his satisfaction before proceeding, and refuse it on failure to comply.
plain_english_summary: Gives the Controller power to refuse non-compliant applications or force amendments as a precondition to further prosecution — an order under this section is appealable to the Appellate Board (now, post-2021, the High Court) under section 117A.

title: Power of Controller to make orders respecting division of application
text: (1) An applicant may, before grant, file a further ('divisional') application in respect of an invention disclosed in the original provisional or complete specification, either voluntarily or to meet a unity-of-invention objection that the claims relate to more than one invention.

sub_structure.2: (2) The divisional application's complete specification cannot include matter not in substance disclosed in the original complete specification.
sub_structure.3_explanation: Explanation: the divisional application and its complete specification are deemed filed on the date of the original (parent) application, and are examined once a request for examination is filed within the prescribed period.

plain_english_summary: The statutory basis for filing 'divisional' patent applications in India — a common strategy for a startup to split out claims covering distinct inventions/technical embodiments from a single parent filing, while retaining the parent's priority date.

title: Power of Controller to make orders respecting dating of application
text: (1) The Controller may, at the applicant's request, post-date an application to a date specified in the request, but not more than six months later than the original (or deemed) filing date.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where amendment of an application/specification/document is required under section 15, it may be deemed made on the date the requirement is complied with, or re-filed.

plain_english_summary: Allows an applicant to voluntarily post-date an application by up to six months, and links non-compliance with amendment requirements to an effective re-dating of the application.

title: Powers of Controller in cases of anticipation
text: (1) Where the invention appears anticipated as described in section 13(1)(a) or 13(2), the Controller may refuse the application unless the applicant shows the claim's priority date predates the relevant publication, or amends the specification to the Controller's satisfaction.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where the invention is claimed in another complete specification under section 13(1)(b), the Controller may direct a cross-reference notice unless the applicant proves an earlier priority date or amends the specification.

plain_english_summary: Gives the Controller tools to resolve anticipation/prior-claim conflicts discovered during the section 13 search, either by refusal, amendment, or a public cross-reference notice between conflicting applications.

title: Powers of Controller in case of potential infringement
text: (1) If it appears an invention cannot be performed without substantial risk of infringing another patent's claim, the Controller may direct a public-notice cross-reference in the applicant's complete specification, unless the applicant shows reasonable grounds to contest the other patent's validity or amends the specification.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller may delete such a cross-reference if the other patent is later revoked, amended to delete the relevant claim, or found invalid/not infringed.

plain_english_summary: Addresses the scenario where a pending application's invention would necessarily infringe an existing patent — the Controller can require a public 'blocking patent' notice rather than refusing the application outright.

title: Powers of Controller to make orders regarding substitution of applicants, etc.
text: (1) Where the Controller is satisfied, on a claim made before grant, that by assignment, written agreement or operation of law a claimant would be entitled to the patent (or a share/interest in it), the Controller may direct that the application proceed in the name of the claimant (with or instead of the original applicant(s)).

sub_structure.2: (2) No such direction may be given by virtue of an assignment by one of several joint applicants except with the others' consent.
sub_structure.4: (4) Where a joint applicant dies before grant, the Controller may, on the survivors' request and with consent of the deceased's legal representative, direct the application to proceed in the survivors' names alone.
sub_structure.5: (5) The Controller may resolve disputes between joint applicants as to how the application should proceed, after hearing all parties.

plain_english_summary: Provides the mechanism to correct or update the named applicant(s) on a pending application through assignment, death, or dispute — directly relevant to a startup that acquires patent rights by assignment from a founder or another company mid-prosecution.

title: Time for putting application in order for grant
text: (1) An application shall be deemed abandoned unless, within the prescribed period (generally 6 months from the first statement of objections, extendable), the applicant has complied with all requirements imposed on him under the Act.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where an appeal to the High Court is pending on the main invention (or, for a patent of addition, on either that or the main invention application), the compliance period is extended until the High Court determines the appeal.
sub_structure.3: (3) If the appeal period has not yet expired, the Controller may extend the compliance period further, subject to any High-Court-granted extension once an appeal is actually filed.

plain_english_summary: Sets the hard deadline by which an applicant must resolve all outstanding objections from the examination process or the application is deemed abandoned — a key prosecution deadline to track, with limited extension avenues tied to pending appeals.

chapter_title: OPPOSITION PROCEEDINGS TO GRANT OF PATENTS
title: Opposition to the patent
text: (1) Where an application has been published but a patent not yet granted, any person may, in writing, represent by way of pre-grant opposition against the grant, on grounds including: (a) wrongful obtaining of the invention; (b) prior publication before the priority date; (c) prior claim in an earlier-priority Indian application; (d) prior public knowledge/use in India; (e) obviousness/lack of inventive step; (f) not an invention or not patentable under the Act; (g) insufficient description; (h) failure to disclose foreign-filing information under section 8; (i) late convention application; (j) non-disclosure/wrong disclosure of biological material's source; (k) anticipation by traditional/indigenous community knowledge.

sub_structure.2: (2) Post-grant opposition: within one year of publication of grant, any person interested may oppose on the same grounds as sub-section (1) (re-numbered for the patentee context).
sub_structure.3: (3) On a post-grant opposition, the Controller constitutes an Opposition Board to examine and recommend, then decides, after hearing both sides, to maintain, amend, or revoke the patent.

plain_english_summary: Creates India's dual pre-grant and post-grant opposition system — any person can oppose before grant (broad standing), while only a 'person interested' can oppose within one year after grant (via an Opposition Board recommendation). This is the main administrative route (short of a court suit) to challenge a rival's software-adjacent or business-method-adjacent patent as invalid, e.g. under the section 3(k) computer-programme-per-se exclusion.

chapter_title: OPPOSITION PROCEEDINGS TO GRANT OF PATENTS
title: In cases of "obtaining" Controller may treat the patent as the patent of opponent
text: (1) Where the Controller finds an invention was wrongfully 'obtained' from the opponent and revokes the patent on that ground, he may, on the opponent's request, direct that the patent stand amended in the opponent's name; where only part of the invention was so obtained, the specification may instead be amended to exclude that part.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where the opponent has a pending patent application covering the wrongfully-obtained invention, the Controller may treat it as filed (for priority-date purposes) on the date the corresponding document was filed by the patentee in the earlier application.

plain_english_summary: A remedy for the person from whom an invention was wrongfully taken (e.g. a co-founder or employee whose invention was misappropriated and patented by someone else) — rather than simply killing the patent, the Controller can transfer it, or preserve priority for the true inventor's own pending application.

chapter_title: OPPOSITION PROCEEDINGS TO GRANT OF PATENTS
title: Mention of inventor as such in patent
text: (1) If satisfied that a person is the inventor (or of a substantial part) of an invention and that the application is a direct consequence of that, the Controller shall cause that person to be mentioned as inventor in the granted patent and the register — though this does not confer or derogate from any patent rights.

sub_structure.2: (2) A request to be mentioned as inventor may be made by the applicant, or jointly by the applicant and the person claiming to be the inventor.
sub_structure.3: (3) A person not covered by such a request may independently claim to be mentioned as inventor.
sub_structure.7: (7) Any person may later apply for a certificate that someone was wrongly mentioned as inventor, and the Controller shall rectify the specification/register accordingly if satisfied.

plain_english_summary: The mechanism for correctly naming inventors on a patent (distinct from ownership/assignee rights) — relevant to startups where the named inventor(s) on the patent (often individual engineers) differ from the patent owner (the company as assignee).

title: Anticipation by previous publication
text: (1) An invention is not deemed anticipated merely because it was published in an Indian patent specification dated before 1 January 1912. (2) Subject to conditions, an invention is not deemed anticipated merely because it was published before the priority date, if the patentee/applicant proves the publication was without consent (obtained from him without authorisation) and, where learned of before filing, that filing followed as soon as reasonably practicable.

sub_structure.3: (3) Where a complete specification is filed by the true and first inventor (or one deriving title from him), the invention is not deemed anticipated merely by a rival application made in contravention of that person's rights, or by subsequent unauthorised use/publication flowing from that rival application.

plain_english_summary: A safe-harbour provision protecting a genuine inventor from having their own invention's unauthorised leak or a bad-faith rival filing used against them as 'prior art' to defeat their own later application — subject to filing promptly after learning of the leak.

title: Anticipation by previous communication to Government
text: An invention is not deemed anticipated merely because of its communication to the Government, or to a person authorised by Government to investigate it, or anything done in consequence of such communication for the purpose of investigation.
plain_english_summary: Protects an inventor who discloses an invention to the Government for evaluation (e.g. a defence or public-sector procurement pitch) from that disclosure being treated as prior art against their own later patent application.

title: Anticipation by public display, etc.
text: An invention is not deemed anticipated merely because of its display (with the true/first inventor's consent) at an official industrial/other exhibition notified by the Central Government, or its use there, or publication describing it in consequence, or use by others during the exhibition without consent, or its description in a paper read before a learned society — provided the patent application is made within twelve months of the exhibition's opening or the paper's reading/publication.
plain_english_summary: A 12-month grace period protecting inventors who showcase an invention at a notified exhibition or academic/professional forum before filing — relevant to startups that demo a prototype at a notified trade show before filing a patent application, though note this grace period applies only to Central-Government-notified exhibitions, not any public demo or conference.

title: Anticipation by public working
text: An invention is not deemed anticipated merely because, within one year before the priority date, it was publicly worked in India by the patentee/applicant (or with their consent) for the purpose of reasonable trial only, where public working was reasonably necessary given the invention's nature.
plain_english_summary: A narrow one-year grace period for public 'reasonable trial' use of an invention in India (e.g. field-testing a hardware/software system in a live environment) before it counts as anticipating prior art.

title: Anticipation by use and publication after provisional specification
text: (1) Where a complete specification follows a provisional specification, the patent shall not be refused, revoked, or invalidated merely because matter described in the provisional specification was used or published in India or elsewhere after the provisional filing date.

sub_structure.2: (2) The same protection applies to matter disclosed in the foreign application underlying a convention application, used/published after that foreign filing date.

plain_english_summary: Protects an applicant's own provisional-specification disclosures (and the disclosures in a foreign priority application) from being used against the later complete specification as intervening prior art — enabling public discussion/use of the invention between provisional filing and complete-specification filing without penalty.

title: No anticipation if circumstances are only as described in sections 29, 30, 31 and 32
text: Notwithstanding anything in the Act, the Controller shall not refuse to grant a patent, and a patent shall not be revoked or invalidated, by reason only of circumstances which, under sections 29 to 32, do not constitute anticipation.
plain_english_summary: A consolidating provision confirming that the various anticipation safe harbours (sections 29-32) apply consistently at every stage — application, grant, and post-grant revocation/invalidation.

chapter_title: PROVISIONS FOR SECRECY OF CERTAIN INVENTIONS
title: Secrecy directions relating to inventions relevant for defence purposes
text: (1) Where an invention appears to the Controller to be relevant for defence purposes (either because it falls within a Central-Government-notified class, or otherwise), he may direct that publication or communication of information about it be prohibited or restricted.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller must notify the Central Government of such directions; if the Government finds publication would not prejudice India's defence, it directs the Controller to revoke the secrecy direction.
sub_structure.3: (3) The Central Government may independently notify the Controller that an un-flagged invention is defence-relevant, triggering the same secrecy-direction regime.

plain_english_summary: Empowers the Patent Office/Government to impose secrecy on defence-relevant inventions, blocking publication — relevant to deep-tech/dual-use software (e.g. cryptography, surveillance, or defence-adjacent AI) startups whose filings could be flagged as defence-sensitive.
