chapter_title: PROVISIONS FOR SECRECY OF CERTAIN INVENTIONS
title: Secrecy directions to be periodically reviewed
text: (1) Whether a secrecy-directed invention remains defence-relevant is reconsidered by the Central Government every six months, or on the applicant's reasonable request, and the direction is revoked if publication would no longer be prejudicial (or, for a foreign applicant, if the invention is published outside India).

sub_structure.2: (2) The result of each reconsideration must be communicated to the applicant within the prescribed time and manner.

plain_english_summary: Ensures secrecy directions under section 35 are not indefinite — mandatory six-monthly review with a right for the applicant to request reconsideration.

chapter_title: PROVISIONS FOR SECRECY OF CERTAIN INVENTIONS
title: Consequences of secrecy directions
text: (1) While a section 35 direction is in force, the Controller cannot refuse the application, and no appeal lies from any order passed in respect of it; the application may proceed up to the grant stage, but is not published and no patent is actually granted while secrecy continues.

sub_structure.2: (2) If the Government uses the invention while secrecy continues, sections 100, 101 and 103 (Government use of inventions) apply as if the patent had been granted; the Central Government may pay a solatium for hardship caused by continued secrecy.
sub_structure.3: (3) No renewal fee is payable for any period during which the secrecy direction was in force.

plain_english_summary: Sets out what happens while an application is under a defence secrecy direction: prosecution is frozen at the pre-grant stage (no refusal, no appeal, no publication, no grant), Government use is compensated as if a patent existed, and no renewal fees accrue.

chapter_title: PROVISIONS FOR SECRECY OF CERTAIN INVENTIONS
title: Revocation of secrecy directions and extension of time
text: When a section 35 direction is revoked, the Controller may, notwithstanding any other time-limit in the Act, extend the time for any step or act in connection with the application, whether or not that time has already expired.
plain_english_summary: Gives the Controller flexibility to reset procedural deadlines once a defence secrecy direction is lifted, so the applicant is not prejudiced by the freeze.

chapter_title: PROVISIONS FOR SECRECY OF CERTAIN INVENTIONS
title: Residents not to apply for patents outside India without prior permission
text: (1) No person resident in India may apply for a patent outside India without a written permit from the Controller, unless a corresponding Indian application was filed at least six weeks earlier and no unrevoked secrecy direction applies.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller must dispose of such permit applications within the prescribed period; for defence/atomic-energy-relevant inventions, the Controller cannot grant a permit without prior Central Government consent.
sub_structure.3: (3) This section does not apply where the first application was filed outside India by a person resident outside India.

plain_english_summary: A foreign-filing-licence requirement: India-resident inventors (including startup founders/employees) generally must file in India first and either wait six weeks or obtain a written permit before filing the same invention abroad — a compliance step easily missed when a startup's IP counsel is based overseas or files first via a foreign parent entity.

chapter_title: PROVISIONS FOR SECRECY OF CERTAIN INVENTIONS
title: Liability for contravention of section 35 or section 39
text: Without prejudice to Chapter XX, if a person contravenes a secrecy direction under section 35, or files a foreign application in contravention of section 39, the Indian application is deemed abandoned and any patent granted is liable to revocation under section 64.
plain_english_summary: The civil/administrative consequence (application abandonment, patent revocation) for breaching the secrecy-direction or foreign-filing-licence rules — separate from, and additional to, the criminal penalty under section 118.

chapter_title: PROVISIONS FOR SECRECY OF CERTAIN INVENTIONS
title: Finality of orders of Controller and Central Government
text: All orders of the Controller giving secrecy directions, and all orders of the Central Government under this Chapter, are final and cannot be questioned in any court on any ground whatsoever.
plain_english_summary: An ouster clause insulating defence-secrecy decisions from judicial review — a notable limitation on an applicant's remedies where national-security secrecy is invoked.

chapter_title: PROVISIONS FOR SECRECY OF CERTAIN INVENTIONS
title: Savings respecting disclosure to Government
text: Nothing in this Act prevents the Controller from disclosing to the Central Government information about an application or specification, for the purpose of it being examined to decide whether a secrecy order should be made or revoked.
plain_english_summary: A narrow carve-out allowing the Controller to share otherwise-confidential application information with the Central Government specifically for secrecy-direction decision-making.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Grant of patents
text: (1) Where an application has been found in order for grant and has not been refused or found in contravention of the Act, the patent shall be granted as expeditiously as possible, with the patent office seal, and the grant date entered in the register.

sub_structure.2: (2) On grant, the Controller shall publish the fact of grant, after which the application, specification and related documents become open for public inspection.

plain_english_summary: The formal grant mechanics — once prosecution concludes favourably, the patent is sealed, dated, registered and published, and the full file becomes publicly inspectable.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Amendment of patent granted to deceased applicant
text: Where the Controller is satisfied that a patent was granted to a person who had already died (or, for a body corporate, ceased to exist) before grant, the Controller may amend the patent to substitute the name of the person to whom it ought to have been granted, with retrospective effect.
plain_english_summary: A corrective mechanism ensuring a patent inadvertently granted to a deceased applicant or defunct company is retrospectively re-attributed to the correct successor/heir.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Date of patent
text: (1) Every patent is dated as of the date the application for the patent was filed. (2) That date is entered in the register.

sub_structure.3: (3) No suit or proceeding can be brought for infringement committed before the date of publication of the application.

plain_english_summary: Confirms a patent's legal date is its filing date, but enforceable infringement liability only starts running from publication of the application (see section 11A) — relevant to calculating the earliest date from which a startup can sue infringers.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Form, extent and effect of patent
text: (1) Every patent shall be in the prescribed form and have effect throughout India. (2) A patent is granted for one invention only.

sub_structure.2_proviso: Proviso: it is not open to any person, in a suit or other proceeding, to object to a patent merely on the ground that it covers more than one invention.

plain_english_summary: Confirms nationwide (all-India) territorial effect of a granted patent, and that a multi-invention patent cannot later be attacked purely on that technical ground.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Grant of patents to be subject to certain conditions
text: Every patent is granted subject to: (1) Government use/import for its own purposes; (2) Government use of a patented process for its own purposes; (3) any person's use for experiment/research purposes, including instructing students; (4) Government import of patented medicines/drugs for its own use or for specified dispensaries/hospitals.
plain_english_summary: Built-in statutory limitations on every Indian patent: a research/experimental-use exemption (relevant to R&D teams testing or reverse-engineering for research) and a Government-use carve-out, both of which apply automatically without needing a licence.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Rights of patentees
text: Subject to the Act and the section 47 conditions, a patent confers on the patentee: (a) for a product, the exclusive right to prevent third parties without consent from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product in India; (b) for a process, the exclusive right to prevent third parties from using that process, and from using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product directly obtained by that process, in India.
plain_english_summary: The core grant of exclusive rights — this is the provision that actually gives a patentee enforceable exclusivity over a patented product or process in India, forming the basis of every patent infringement claim under Chapter XVIII.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Patent rights not infringed when used on foreign vessels etc., temporarily or accidentally in India
text: (1) Where a foreign-registered vessel, aircraft, or land vehicle owned by a foreign resident comes into India temporarily or accidentally, use of a patented invention in its body/machinery/construction (for its own actual needs) is not deemed infringement.

sub_structure.2: (2) This exemption does not extend to countries whose laws do not offer India reciprocal treatment for its own vessels/aircraft/vehicles.

plain_english_summary: A narrow international-comity exemption for patented technology embedded in foreign transport passing through India temporarily, subject to reciprocity.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Rights of co-owners of patents
text: (1) Where a patent is granted to two or more persons, each is entitled to an equal undivided share absent a contrary agreement. (2) Absent agreement otherwise, each co-owner may exercise section 48 rights for their own benefit without accounting to the others.

sub_structure.3: (3) A licence cannot be granted, nor a share assigned, by one co-owner without the others' consent, subject to any governing agreement.
sub_structure.4: (4) A purchaser of a patented article sold by one co-owner may deal with it as if bought from a sole patentee.

plain_english_summary: Default rules for jointly-owned patents (e.g. where two co-founders or a startup and a university are co-applicants) — each co-owner can independently exploit the patent without accounting to others, but cannot license or assign a share without consent, making a co-ownership/joint-development agreement important to override these defaults.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Power of Controller to give directions to co-owners
text: (1) The Controller may, on application by any co-owner, give directions as to sale/lease of the patent, licence grants, or exercise of section 50 rights.

sub_structure.2: (2) If a co-owner fails to execute a required instrument within 14 days of being requested, the Controller may empower another person to execute it on the defaulter's behalf.

plain_english_summary: A dispute-resolution backstop where co-owners of a patent (e.g. joint-venture partners) cannot agree on licensing or dealing with the patent, allowing the Controller to break the deadlock.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Grant of patent to true and first inventor where it has been obtained by another in fraud of him
text: (1) Where a patent is revoked under section 64 for having been wrongfully/fraudulently obtained from the petitioner, the Appellate Board or court may, in the same proceeding, permit grant of the whole or relevant part of the invention to the petitioner instead.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller then grants a new patent (same date/number, or a modified number for a partial grant) to the petitioner, potentially requiring a fresh complete specification.

plain_english_summary: A remedy allowing the true inventor whose invention was fraudulently patented by someone else to obtain the patent themselves, in the same revocation proceeding, rather than starting a fresh application from scratch.

chapter_title: GRANT OF PATENTS AND RIGHTS CONFERRED THEREBY
title: Term of patent
text: (1) The term of every patent granted after the commencement of the Patents (Amendment) Act, 2002 (and every unexpired patent as of that date) is twenty years from the date of filing of the application (or, for PCT international applications designating India, twenty years from the international filing date).

sub_structure.2: (2) A patent ceases to have effect if the prescribed renewal fee is not paid within the prescribed (or extended) period.
sub_structure.4: (4) On cesser for non-payment or expiry of term, the subject matter loses all protection under the patent — it falls into the public domain.

plain_english_summary: Establishes India's uniform 20-year patent term (from filing date, not grant date) — this is a defining TRIPS-compliance provision from the 2002 amendment, and it is critical for a startup to track annual renewal-fee deadlines since non-payment causes automatic lapse and loss of all exclusivity.

title: Patents of addition
text: (1) Where an application is for an improvement or modification of an invention already applied for or patented by the same applicant (the 'main invention'), the Controller may, at the applicant's request, grant it as a patent of addition.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where an improvement/modification patent is independently held by the same patentee as the main invention, the Controller may, at the patentee's request, revoke it and re-grant it as a patent of addition dated as of the revoked patent.
sub_structure.3: (3) A patent of addition cannot be granted unless its filing date is the same as or later than the main invention's filing date.
sub_structure.4: (4) A patent of addition cannot be granted before the main invention's patent is granted.

plain_english_summary: A mechanism for patenting incremental improvements to an already-patented (or already-applied-for) invention as a linked 'patent of addition', useful for startups that iterate on a core patented technology and want follow-on protection without a fresh inventive-step fight against the parent patent (see section 56).

title: Term of patents of addition
text: (1) A patent of addition is granted for a term equal to the (remaining) term of the main invention's patent, and lapses with it — unless the main patent is revoked, in which case the court/Controller may convert the addition into an independent patent for the main patent's remaining term.

sub_structure.2: (2) No renewal fees are payable for a patent of addition, but if it becomes independent, standard renewal fees become payable thereafter.

plain_english_summary: A patent of addition normally rides on the coattails of the main patent's term and fee schedule (no separate renewal fees) but can be converted into a stand-alone patent if the main patent is later revoked.

title: Validity of patents of addition
text: (1) A patent of addition cannot be refused, revoked, or invalidated merely for lacking inventive step over the main invention (or over other addition patents to it); nor can its validity be questioned merely because it ought to have been an independent patent.

sub_structure.2: (2) In assessing novelty of a patent-of-addition application, the main invention's complete specification is also considered.

plain_english_summary: Insulates a patent of addition from the specific attack that it is 'obvious' in light of its own main invention — the whole point of the addition-patent mechanism being to protect improvements that build directly on a patentee's own prior invention.

title: Amendment of application and specification or any document relating thereto before Controller
text: (1) Subject to section 59, the Controller may, on application by an applicant/patentee, allow amendment of the application, complete specification, or related document, subject to conditions — but cannot rule on such an amendment while an infringement suit or revocation proceeding on the same patent is pending.

sub_structure.3: (3) Post-grant amendment applications and their nature may be published.
sub_structure.4: (4) After publication, any interested person may oppose within the prescribed period, triggering a hearing before the Controller decides.

plain_english_summary: The general route for amending a pending application or a granted patent's specification before the Controller — amendments are frozen while litigation is pending (to prevent tactical claim-shifting mid-suit) and post-grant amendments are publicly opposable.

title: Amendment of specification before Appellate Board or High Court
text: (1) In revocation proceedings before the Appellate Board or High Court, subject to section 59, the tribunal may allow the patentee to amend the complete specification, and may allow amendment instead of revoking an invalid patent.

sub_structure.3: (3) Copies of allowed amendment orders are transmitted to the Controller, who must register the amendment.

plain_english_summary: Allows a patentee facing a revocation challenge to save the patent by amending the specification (e.g. narrowing claims) instead of losing it entirely — a key defensive tool in patent litigation.

title: Supplementary provisions as to amendment of application or specification
text: (1) No amendment is allowed except by way of disclaimer, correction or explanation, for incorporating actual fact, and no amendment may add matter not in substance already disclosed, nor may an amended claim fall outside the scope of a pre-amendment claim (no broadening).

sub_structure.2: (2) Post-grant amendments become part of the specification, must be published, and cannot be challenged except on the ground of fraud.

plain_english_summary: The critical substantive limit on all patent amendments in India: no new matter, and amended claims cannot broaden beyond the pre-amendment claim scope — a strict added-matter/no-broadening rule that shapes how claims can be salvaged during prosecution or litigation.

title: Applications for restoration of lapsed patents
text: (1) Where a patent has lapsed for non-payment of a renewal fee, the patentee (or legal representative, or, with leave, one of several joint patentees) may apply for restoration within eighteen months of the lapse.

sub_structure.3: (3) The application must contain a verified statement of the circumstances of the failure to pay, and the Controller may require further evidence.

plain_english_summary: Gives a startup that inadvertently lets a patent lapse for missing a renewal-fee deadline an eighteen-month window to apply for restoration, provided the failure was unintentional (see section 61).

title: Procedure for disposal of applications for restoration of lapsed patents
text: (1) If prima facie satisfied the non-payment was unintentional and there was no undue delay in applying, the Controller publishes the restoration application; any interested person may oppose on the grounds that the failure was not unintentional or that there was undue delay.

sub_structure.3: (3) If unopposed, or if the Controller decides in the applicant's favour, the patent (and any patent of addition) is restored on payment of unpaid and additional prescribed fees.

plain_english_summary: Sets the public, opposable procedure for restoring a lapsed patent — a competitor who began using the invention during the lapse period can oppose restoration or otherwise gain protections under section 62.

title: Rights of patentees of lapsed patents which have been restored
text: (1) On restoration, the patentee's rights are subject to prescribed provisions and any conditions the Controller imposes to protect or compensate persons who began (or took definite steps) to use the invention during the lapse period.

sub_structure.2: (2) No infringement suit may be brought for use of the invention between the lapse date and the date the restoration application was published.

plain_english_summary: Protects third parties who started using a lapsed invention in good faith during the gap before restoration — a restored patent cannot be used to sue for that intervening-period use, and the Controller may impose ongoing protective conditions (an 'intervening rights' regime).

title: Surrender of patents
text: (1) A patentee may, by notice to the Controller, offer to surrender the patent. (2) The Controller publishes the offer and notifies all persons with a registered interest in the patent.

sub_structure.3: (3) Any interested person may oppose the surrender within the prescribed period.
sub_structure.4: (4) If satisfied the patent may properly be surrendered (after hearing the patentee and any opponent), the Controller accepts the offer and revokes the patent.

plain_english_summary: The voluntary route for a patentee to give up a patent (e.g. one no longer commercially useful), subject to public notice and a right for interested third parties (such as licensees) to oppose the surrender.

title: Revocation of patents
text: (1) A patent may be revoked on a petition by any person interested or the Central Government before the Appellate Board, or on a counter-claim in an infringement suit before the High Court, on grounds including: (a) prior claim of earlier priority; (b) grant to a non-entitled applicant; (c) wrongful obtaining; (d) not an invention; (e) lack of novelty; (f) obviousness/lack of inventive step; (g) not useful; (h) insufficient description; (i) unclear/unsupported claims; (j) false suggestion/representation; (k) not patentable under the Act; (l) prior secret use in India; (m) non-disclosure of foreign filings under section 8; (n) contravention of secrecy directions (sections 35/39); (o) fraudulently obtained amendment; (p) wrong disclosure of biological material source; (q) anticipation by traditional/indigenous knowledge.

sub_structure.4: (4) The High Court may also revoke a patent, on the Central Government's petition, where the patentee unreasonably refused a Government request to work the invention for Government purposes under section 99.
sub_structure.5: (5) Notice of a revocation petition must be served on all registered proprietors/interest-holders.

plain_english_summary: The comprehensive list of grounds on which any Indian patent can be revoked (post-grant), including 'not patentable under this Act' (clause (k)), which is exactly the hook used to revoke a software patent that should have been excluded under section 3(k) — the mirror-image, post-grant version of the pre/post-grant opposition grounds in section 25.

title: Revocation of patent or amendment of complete specification on directions from Government in cases relating to atomic energy
text: (1) Where the Central Government is satisfied a granted patent is for an atomic-energy invention barred under section 20(1) of the Atomic Energy Act, 1962, it may direct the Controller to revoke it, after notice and hearing to the patentee and interested parties.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller may instead allow the patentee to amend the specification, rather than revoking the patent.

plain_english_summary: A sector-specific revocation power mirroring the non-patentability bar in section 4, applicable when an atomic-energy patent slips through examination.

title: Revocation of patent in public interest
text: Where the Central Government considers a patent, or how it is exercised, mischievous to the State or generally prejudicial to the public, it may, after giving the patentee a hearing, declare the patent revoked by notification in the Official Gazette.
plain_english_summary: A broad public-interest revocation power exercisable directly by the Central Government (via Gazette declaration) without a court/Board proceeding — an extraordinary override reserved for patents whose exercise is harmful to the State or public.

title: Register of patents and particulars to be entered therein
text: (1) A register of patents shall be kept at the patent office, recording: (a) names/addresses of grantees; (b) assignment, extension and revocation notifications; (c) other prescribed particulars affecting validity/proprietorship.

sub_structure.2: (2) No notice of any trust (express, implied or constructive) shall be entered, and the Controller is unaffected by such notices.
sub_structure.4: (4) The register may be kept in electronic form (computer floppies/diskettes or other electronic form) subject to prescribed safeguards.
sub_structure.5: (5) A certified copy of, or extract from, the register is admissible in evidence in all legal proceedings notwithstanding the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

plain_english_summary: Establishes the official patent register as the authoritative public record of ownership, assignments and interests — an early (2002 amendment) recognition of electronic recordkeeping, and certified extracts serve as self-authenticating evidence in litigation.

title: Assignments, etc., not to be valid unless in writing and duly executed
text: An assignment of a patent or a share in it, a mortgage, licence, or the creation of any other interest in a patent, is not valid unless in writing, reduced to a document embodying all agreed terms and conditions, and duly executed by the parties.
plain_english_summary: The formal-validity rule for ALL patent transactions — assignments, mortgages, AND licences — must be a single written, duly executed instrument covering all agreed terms; an oral or informally-documented patent licence or assignment is simply invalid under Indian law, making this essential boilerplate compliance for any software/IP licensing deal involving a patent.

title: Registration of assignments, transmissions, etc.
text: (1) A person who becomes entitled by assignment, transmission or operation of law to a patent, share, or other interest (e.g. as mortgagee or licensee) must apply to register their title or interest.

sub_structure.3: (3) On proof of title, the Controller registers the person as proprietor/co-proprietor (for ownership) or enters notice of interest (for other interests); if there's a dispute over validity of the transaction, the Controller may defer registration pending court determination.
sub_structure.4: (4) Copies of agreements/licences/other title documents must be supplied to the Controller for filing; for a licence, the patentee/licensee may request that its terms not be disclosed except by court order.
sub_structure.5: (5) An unregistered document generally cannot be admitted as evidence of title (other than for the registration/rectification application itself), absent special reasons.

plain_english_summary: The recordal regime for patent assignments/licences — registering the assignment or licence at the Patent Office is what makes the title/interest enforceable and usable as evidence, and licence terms can be kept confidential from public inspection on request, which is directly relevant when structuring and recording a patent licence agreement.

title: Power of registered grantee or proprietor to deal with patent
text: Subject to co-ownership rules and any registered third-party rights, the registered grantee/proprietor of a patent may assign, license, or otherwise deal with it and give effectual receipts for any consideration.
plain_english_summary: Confirms that registration as proprietor gives full power to assign, license or otherwise commercially exploit the patent — the basic statutory authority underlying every patent sale or licensing transaction.

title: Rectification of register by Appellate Board
text: (1) The Appellate Board may, on application by an aggrieved person, order the making, variation, or deletion of a register entry that is absent/omitted, wrongly made, wrongly remaining, or erroneous/defective.

sub_structure.3: (3) Notice must be given to the Controller, who is entitled to appear and be heard, and must appear if directed.

plain_english_summary: The mechanism to correct errors in the official patent register (e.g. an incorrect ownership entry) via the Appellate Board (now, post-2021, effectively the High Court) rather than the Controller directly.

title: Register to be open for inspection
text: (1) Subject to the Act and rules, the register shall be open to public inspection at all convenient times, and certified copies of entries given on payment of the prescribed fee.

sub_structure.2: (2) The register is prima facie evidence of matters required to be entered in it.

plain_english_summary: Confirms the patent register's public-inspection status — useful for a startup's freedom-to-operate or ownership due-diligence checks before a licensing deal or M&A transaction.

title: Controller and other officers
text: (1) The Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks appointed under the Trade Marks Act, 1999 shall be the Controller of Patents. (2) The Central Government may appoint examiners and other officers as it thinks fit.

sub_structure.4: (4) The Controller may, by written order, withdraw a pending matter from an officer and deal with it himself (de novo or from that stage) or transfer it to another officer.

plain_english_summary: Establishes the single Controller General office spanning patents, designs and trade marks, and the delegation/withdrawal powers governing how individual patent examiners handle applications.

title: Patent office and its branches
text: (1) There shall be an office known as the patent office. (2)-(3) The Central Government specifies its name and the location of the head office, and may establish branch offices. (4) There shall be a seal of the patent office.
plain_english_summary: The institutional/administrative basis for the Indian Patent Office and its branch offices (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata) and official seal.

title: Restriction on employees of patent office as to right or interest in patents
text: All patent office officers and employees are incapable, during their tenure, of acquiring or taking (directly or indirectly, except by inheritance or bequest) any right or interest in any patent issued by that office.
plain_english_summary: A conflict-of-interest rule barring patent examiners/officials from holding a personal stake in any patent granted by their own office.

title: Officers and employees not to furnish information, etc.
text: A patent office officer/employee shall not, except when authorised by the Act, the Central Government, the Appellate Board, the Controller, or court order— (a) furnish information on a pending/dealt matter; (b) prepare or assist in preparing a document for filing; or (c) conduct a records search.
plain_english_summary: A confidentiality/impartiality rule preventing patent office staff from moonlighting as informal patent agents or leaking application information outside official channels.

title: Controller to have certain powers of a civil court
text: (1) The Controller, in proceedings before him, has civil-court powers under the CPC 1908 for: summoning/examining witnesses on oath; requiring discovery/production of documents; receiving affidavit evidence; issuing commissions for examination; awarding costs; reviewing his own decisions; setting aside ex-parte orders; and any other prescribed matter.

sub_structure.2: (2) Any costs order by the Controller is executable as a civil court decree.

plain_english_summary: Gives the Controller quasi-judicial powers (summons, discovery, affidavits, costs) — relevant to how opposition, compulsory-licence, and other contested Patent Office proceedings are actually conducted.

title: Power of Controller to correct clerical errors etc.
text: (1) Subject to sections 57, 59 and 44, the Controller may correct clerical errors in a patent, specification, related document, application, or register entry.

sub_structure.4: (4) Where a requested correction would materially alter meaning/scope and could affect third parties, the Controller must require publication of the proposed correction, allowing opposition.

plain_english_summary: A lighter-weight route (distinct from formal amendment under sections 57-59) for fixing purely clerical mistakes, with public notice required where the correction is substantively significant.

title: Evidence how to be given and powers of Controller in respect thereof
text: Subject to rules, evidence in Patent Office proceedings is normally given by affidavit, but the Controller may take oral evidence instead of/in addition, or allow cross-examination on an affidavit's contents.
plain_english_summary: Sets the default evidentiary procedure (affidavit-based) for contested Patent Office proceedings, with Controller discretion to allow oral evidence/cross-examination.

title: Exercise of discretionary powers by Controller
text: The Controller must give an applicant (for a patent or specification amendment) an opportunity to be heard before exercising any discretion adversely to them, if the applicant timely requests a hearing.

sub_structure.proviso: Proviso: the hearing request must be made at least ten days before expiry of the relevant time-limit.

plain_english_summary: A natural-justice safeguard requiring the Controller to hear an applicant before any adverse discretionary decision, provided the applicant asks in time.

title: Disposal by Controller of applications for extension of time
text: Where the Controller may extend time for doing any act under the Act or rules, nothing requires him to notify or hear anyone opposing the extension, and no appeal lies from an order granting such extension.
plain_english_summary: Time-extension orders are made at the Controller's sole discretion without a hearing requirement for opponents, and are unappealable — a practical procedural point for managing prosecution deadlines.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Definition of "patented articles" and "patentee"
text: In this Chapter, unless the context otherwise requires: (a) "patented article" includes any article made by a patented process; (b) "patentee" includes an exclusive licensee.
plain_english_summary: Extends the compulsory-licensing chapter's scope so that an exclusive licensee (not just the registered patentee) is treated as 'patentee' for these purposes — relevant where a startup holds an exclusive licence rather than outright ownership.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: General principles applicable to working of patented inventions
text: In exercising Chapter XVI powers, regard shall be had to: (a) patents exist to encourage inventions worked commercially in India; (b) not merely to enable import monopolies; (c) that patent protection should promote technology transfer/dissemination to mutual advantage; (d) that patents must not impede public health/nutrition protection; (e) that patents don't restrict Government public-health measures; (f) that patent rights are not abused or used to unreasonably restrain trade/international technology transfer; (g) that patented inventions be available at reasonably affordable prices.
plain_english_summary: The policy 'north star' guiding every compulsory-licensing and revocation-for-non-working decision under this Chapter — India's patent system is explicitly framed around local working, affordability, and preventing abuse of monopoly, which is the backdrop against which any FRAND-style or open-source-adjacent compulsory-licensing dispute involving a software-related patent would be assessed.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Compulsory licences
text: (1) After three years from grant, any interested person may apply for a compulsory licence on the grounds that: (a) reasonable public requirements for the invention are unsatisfied; (b) the invention is not available to the public at a reasonably affordable price; or (c) the invention is not worked in India.

sub_structure.6: (6) In deciding, the Controller considers the invention's nature, time elapsed, the applicant's ability/capacity to work it, and whether the applicant tried and failed to get a licence on reasonable terms (this last factor does not apply in national emergencies, extreme urgency, public non-commercial use, or established anti-competitive conduct by the patentee).
sub_structure.7_selected: (7) 'Reasonable requirements of the public' are deemed unsatisfied where, e.g., the patentee's refusal to license prejudices trade/industry or unmet demand; or conditions on licensing/purchase prejudice unrelated trade; or the patentee imposes exclusive grant-back, no-challenge, or coercive package-licensing conditions; or the invention isn't commercially worked in India to the fullest practicable extent; or Indian working is blocked by the patentee's own imports.

plain_english_summary: India's central compulsory-licensing provision (used, notably, in the 2012 Natco v. Bayer case) — it lets any interested party force a licence three years after grant if the patent isn't being worked in India, isn't affordably priced, or public demand isn't met, and explicitly treats 'coercive package licensing', 'no-challenge' clauses, and exclusive grant-back conditions as signs of abuse. This is the backdrop against which FRAND-style disputes over standard-essential software/hardware patents, or disputes over refusal to license open technical standards, would play out in India.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Revocation of patents by the Controller for non-working
text: (1) Where a compulsory licence has been granted, the Central Government or any interested person may, after two years from that order, apply to revoke the patent on grounds that the invention remains unworked in India, public requirements remain unsatisfied, or pricing remains unaffordable.

sub_structure.4: (4) Applications under this section should ordinarily be decided within one year.

plain_english_summary: The escalation beyond a compulsory licence — if two years after a compulsory licence the underlying problems (non-working, unmet demand, unaffordable pricing) persist, the patent itself can be revoked outright.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Power of Controller to adjourn applications for compulsory licences, etc., in certain cases
text: (1) Where a compulsory-licence/revocation application is based on non-working and the Controller finds insufficient time has elapsed to enable commercial working, he may adjourn the hearing for up to twelve months to allow working to occur.

sub_structure.2: (2) No adjournment is granted unless the Controller is satisfied the patentee has taken prompt, adequate steps to start working the invention in India.

plain_english_summary: A grace mechanism letting a patentee who is genuinely trying to commercialise in India buy up to twelve months before facing a compulsory-licence/revocation order for non-working, provided they show real effort.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Procedure for dealing with applications under sections 84 and 85
text: (1) Where a prima facie case is made out, the Controller directs the applicant to serve the application on the patentee and other interested registrants, and publishes it in the official journal.

sub_structure.2: (2) The patentee (or others) may oppose within the prescribed time, with the opposition notice stating the grounds relied on.

plain_english_summary: The procedural roadmap for contested compulsory-licence and non-working-revocation applications — public notice, service on the patentee, and a formal opposition/hearing process.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Powers of Controller in granting compulsory licences
text: (1) Where unprotected-material manufacture/use/sale is prejudiced by the patentee's licensing/purchase conditions, the Controller may order licences to the applicant's customers as well as the applicant.

sub_structure.3: (3) Where an applicant needs a compulsory licence under multiple related patents held by the same patentee to work the licensed invention without infringing the others, and those other patents represent important technical advancement, the Controller may extend the compulsory licence to cover them too.

plain_english_summary: Gives the Controller flexibility to extend a compulsory licence's practical scope — including to related/blocking patents held by the same patentee — so the licensee can actually exploit the invention without stepping on other patents in the same portfolio.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: General purposes for granting compulsory licences
text: Controller powers under section 84 are exercised to secure: (a) that patented inventions are worked commercially in India without undue delay and to the fullest practicable extent; (b) that the interests of anyone already working/developing the invention in India under the patent's protection are not unfairly prejudiced.
plain_english_summary: States the twin policy goals balancing compulsory licensing: promote actual Indian commercial working, while not unfairly undermining those already investing in working the invention.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Terms and conditions of compulsory licences
text: (1) In settling terms, the Controller endeavours to secure: reasonable royalty; the invention worked to the fullest extent with reasonable profit to the licensee; affordable pricing to the public; a non-exclusive, non-assignable licence; a term for the balance of the patent (unless a shorter term suits the public interest); a predominant focus on the Indian market (with limited export allowance); public non-commercial use for semiconductor technology; and export permission where the licence remedies anti-competitive conduct.

sub_structure.2: (2) No compulsory licence may authorise importing the patented article/product from abroad in a way that would otherwise infringe the patentee's rights.
sub_structure.3: (3) The Central Government may, in the public interest, direct the Controller to authorise a compulsory licensee to import the patented article/product, on specified conditions (royalty, quantum, price, period).

plain_english_summary: Sets the mandatory shape of every compulsory licence in India: non-exclusive, non-assignable, reasonable royalty, primarily for domestic supply, with narrow carve-outs for semiconductor technology (public non-commercial use only) and anti-competitive-remedy cases (export permitted) — a detailed template relevant when negotiating or contesting compulsory licence terms.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Licensing of related patents
text: (1) A person entitled to work another patented invention (as patentee or licensee) may apply for a compulsory licence of a first patent on the ground that they are prevented/hindered, without it, from efficiently working the other invention.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller must be satisfied the applicant is able/willing to reciprocally license the other invention on reasonable terms, and that the other invention substantially contributes to Indian commercial/industrial development.

plain_english_summary: A cross-licensing compulsory mechanism for interdependent/blocking patents held by different parties — relevant to standard-essential-patent-style disputes where two parties each hold patents the other needs to work its own invention.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Special provision for compulsory licences on notifications by Central Government
text: (1) In a declared national emergency, extreme urgency, or case of public non-commercial use, the Central Government may notify that compulsory licences should be available for a patent, whereupon the Controller must grant licences to any interested applicant on such terms as he thinks fit, endeavouring to make patented articles available to the public at the lowest price consistent with a reasonable return to the patentee.

sub_structure.3: (3) For public health crises (e.g. HIV/AIDS, TB, malaria, other epidemics) or emergencies/urgency, the normal section 87 opposition procedure is dispensed with — the Controller informs the patentee but need not run the standard contested process.

plain_english_summary: The fast-track, government-declared compulsory licensing mechanism for national emergencies and public-health crises — bypassing the normal contested opposition procedure — the most powerful compulsory-licensing tool in the Act, directly analogous to how governments have used similar mechanisms for essential medicines and could, in principle, be invoked for critical software/technology infrastructure in an emergency.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Compulsory licence for export of patented pharmaceutical products in certain exceptional circumstances
text: (1) A compulsory licence is available for manufacture and export of patented pharmaceutical products to a country with insufficient/no manufacturing capacity, to address public health problems, provided that importing country has granted a compulsory licence or otherwise permits such import.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller grants such an export-only compulsory licence on application, under specified terms.
sub_structure.explanation: Explanation: 'pharmaceutical products' includes ingredients necessary for manufacture and diagnostic kits required for use.

plain_english_summary: India's implementation of the WTO 'Paragraph 6' mechanism (Doha Declaration) allowing compulsory-licensed generic manufacture in India specifically for export to countries unable to manufacture medicines themselves — a narrow pharma-specific export compulsory licence.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Order for licence to operate as a deed between parties concerned
text: Any order granting a licence under this Chapter operates as if it were a deed of licence executed by the patentee and all necessary parties, embodying the Controller's settled terms and conditions.
plain_english_summary: A compulsory-licence order is self-executing — it has the same legal force as a formally signed licence deed, without needing the patentee's actual signature.

chapter_title: WORKING OF PATENTS, COMPULSORY LICENCES AND REVOCATION
title: Termination of compulsory licence
text: (1) On application by the patentee or another interested party, the Controller may terminate a section 84 compulsory licence once the circumstances that justified it no longer exist and are unlikely to recur — subject to the licensee's right to object.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller must ensure the previously-licensed party's interests are not unduly prejudiced in deciding termination.

plain_english_summary: Compulsory licences are not necessarily permanent — once the underlying justification (e.g. non-working or unaffordability) is resolved, the patentee can apply to end the compulsory licence, balanced against the licensee's reliance interests.

chapter_title: USE OF INVENTIONS FOR PURPOSES OF GOVERNMENT AND ACQUISITION OF INVENTIONS BY CENTRAL GOVERNMENT
title: Meaning of use of invention for purposes of Government
text: (1) For this Chapter, an invention is 'used for the purposes of Government' if made, used, exercised or vended for the Central Government, a State Government, or a Government undertaking.

sub_structure.3: (3) This Chapter does not apply to importation/making/using that is already permitted under the section 47 conditions.

plain_english_summary: Defines the scope of 'Government use' that triggers the Chapter XVII compensation regime — covers Central, State, and Government-undertaking use.

chapter_title: USE OF INVENTIONS FOR PURPOSES OF GOVERNMENT AND ACQUISITION OF INVENTIONS BY CENTRAL GOVERNMENT
title: Power of Central Government to use inventions for purposes of Government
text: (1) The Central Government (and anyone it authorises) may use a patented invention (or one under a pending application) for Government purposes at any time after filing or grant.

sub_structure.2: (2) If the invention was already recorded/tested/tried by or for Government before the priority date (not via the patentee's disclosure), such Government use may be royalty-free.
sub_structure.3: (3) Otherwise, Government use must be on agreed terms or, absent agreement, terms fixed by the High Court under section 103, with the patentee entitled to adequate (not excessive) remuneration.
sub_structure.5: (5) The Government must notify the patentee of such use (except in emergencies/non-commercial use) and provide reasonably requested information on the extent of use.

plain_english_summary: The Government's 'eminent domain'-style right to use any patented invention (including software-related inventions) for its own purposes, with compensation set by agreement or by the High Court if unresolved — relevant to companies selling patented technology into government procurement.

chapter_title: USE OF INVENTIONS FOR PURPOSES OF GOVERNMENT AND ACQUISITION OF INVENTIONS BY CENTRAL GOVERNMENT
title: Rights of third parties in respect of use of invention for purposes of Government
text: (1) Where an invention is used for Government purposes (by Government, its authorised persons, or the patentee on Government order), any private licence/assignment/agreement term restricting or regulating such Government use, or requiring payment for it, is of no effect for that Government use; reproducing/publishing a model or document for that Government use is not copyright infringement.

sub_structure.3: (3) Where payments are due under section 100(3) and there is an exclusive licensee authorised for Government-purpose use, the payment is shared between patentee and licensee by agreement or, in default, as the High Court determines.

plain_english_summary: Overrides private licence terms (including exclusivity and no-Government-use clauses) to the extent they would restrict or charge for the Government's own statutory right of use — a limitation every patent licensing agreement implicitly operates subject to.

chapter_title: USE OF INVENTIONS FOR PURPOSES OF GOVERNMENT AND ACQUISITION OF INVENTIONS BY CENTRAL GOVERNMENT
title: Acquisition of inventions and patents by the Central Government
text: (1) The Central Government may, for a public purpose, publish a notification acquiring an invention/patent, upon which it (and all related rights) vest in the Central Government by force of the notification.

sub_structure.3: (3) Compensation is paid to the applicant/patentee (and other registered interest-holders) as agreed, or, in default, as fixed by the High Court under section 103, having regard to expenditure, term, and prior profits.

plain_english_summary: A compulsory-acquisition power letting Government outright expropriate a patent (with compensation), going further than the mere royalty-bearing 'use' right under section 100 — an extreme but real risk for any patent covering technology of significant public interest.

chapter_title: USE OF INVENTIONS FOR PURPOSES OF GOVERNMENT AND ACQUISITION OF INVENTIONS BY CENTRAL GOVERNMENT
title: Reference to High Court of disputes as to use for purposes of Government
text: (1) Disputes over the Central Government's exercise of section 100 powers, terms of Government use, entitlement to payment shares, or compensation for acquisition under section 102, may be referred to the High Court.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Central Government may, in such proceedings, counter-claim for revocation or otherwise put patent validity in issue.
sub_structure.6: (6) Where the invention was made by a Government/Government-undertaking employee in the course of duty, disputes under this section are instead resolved by the Central Government itself (after a hearing), not the High Court.

plain_english_summary: The dispute-resolution forum (the High Court, with a special carve-out for Government-employee inventions resolved by the Government itself) for Government-use and acquisition compensation disputes under this Chapter.

title: Jurisdiction
text: No suit for a declaration under section 105, relief under section 106, or patent infringement, may be instituted in any court below a district court having jurisdiction.

sub_structure.proviso: Proviso: where the defendant counter-claims for revocation, the suit and counter-claim are transferred to the High Court for decision.

plain_english_summary: Sets the minimum court level (district court) for patent litigation, with an automatic escalation to the High Court whenever the defendant raises a revocation counter-claim — the standard jurisdictional gateway for any Indian patent infringement suit, including one involving a software-related patent.

title: Burden of proof in case of suits concerning infringement
text: (1) In a process-patent infringement suit, the court may direct the defendant to prove their process differs from the patented process, if either the patented process is for obtaining a new product, or there is a substantial likelihood the identical product was made by the patented process and the patentee, despite reasonable efforts, could not determine the actual process used (subject to the patentee first proving the products are identical).

sub_structure.2: (2) In assessing whether this burden has been discharged, the court shall not require disclosure of manufacturing/commercial secrets if that would be unreasonable.

plain_english_summary: A TRIPS-mandated reverse burden of proof for process-patent infringement — once the patentee shows an identical product exists and a new/hard-to-detect process is plausibly involved, the defendant must prove they used a different process, while courts are directed to protect the defendant's trade secrets during that process.

title: Power of court to make declaration as to non-infringement
text: (1) Notwithstanding section 34 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, any person may sue for a declaration that their process/product does not infringe a patent, even without an assertion to the contrary by the patentee, provided they first sought (in writing, with full particulars) a written acknowledgement from the patentee/exclusive licensee, which was refused or ignored.

sub_structure.2: (2) Costs of such a declaratory suit are normally borne by the plaintiff unless the court orders otherwise.
sub_structure.3: (3) A patent's validity cannot be contested in this declaratory suit, and the outcome doesn't imply the patent is valid or invalid.

plain_english_summary: India's 'clearance'/declaratory-judgment mechanism — lets a company proactively seek court confirmation that its product/process does NOT infringe a specific patent (useful before launching a competing software/hardware product), but only after first formally requesting (and being refused) written confirmation from the patentee directly.

title: Power of court to grant relief in cases of groundless threats of infringement proceedings
text: (1) Where any person threatens another (by circulars, ads, or communications) with patent infringement proceedings, the threatened person may sue for: (a) a declaration the threats are unjustifiable; (b) an injunction against continuing the threats; and (c) damages sustained.

sub_structure.2: (2) Relief is granted unless the defendant proves the threatened acts would actually infringe a valid, unchallenged claim.
sub_structure.explanation: Explanation: merely notifying someone of a patent's existence is not a 'threat' under this section.

plain_english_summary: An anti-bullying provision against groundless patent-infringement threats — directly relevant where a patent holder sends aggressive cease-and-desist letters to a startup's customers/partners without a real infringement case; the recipient can sue back for a declaration, injunction and damages, unless the threatener proves genuine infringement.

title: Defences, etc., in suits for infringement
text: (1) In an infringement suit, every ground on which the patent could be revoked under section 64 is available as a defence.

sub_structure.2: (2) It is also a defence that the alleged infringing making/using/importation/distribution was within the section 47 conditions (e.g. Government use, research/experimental use).

plain_english_summary: Confirms that invalidity (any section 64 ground, including the section 3(k) software/algorithm exclusion) is always available as a full defence in an infringement suit, plus the statutory research-use exemption as a separate defence.

title: Certain acts not to be considered as infringement
text: (a) Making, constructing, using, selling or importing a patented invention solely for uses reasonably related to developing and submitting information required under any law (in India or elsewhere) regulating manufacture, construction, use, sale or import of a product, is not infringement. (b) Importing patented products from a person duly authorised by law to produce and sell/distribute them is not infringement.
plain_english_summary: India's 'Bolar exemption' (clause (a) — allows regulatory-approval-related testing/use of a patented invention without infringing, e.g. generic drug trials before patent expiry, but drafted broadly enough to cover regulatory testing of other patented technologies too) and international/parallel-import exhaustion rule (clause (b) — importing genuine patented goods from an authorised producer elsewhere is not infringement), both introduced by the 2005 TRIPS amendment.

title: Reliefs in suit for infringement
text: (1) Reliefs available include an injunction (on such terms as the court thinks fit) and, at the plaintiff's election, either damages or an account of profits.

sub_structure.2: (2) The court may order infringing goods, and materials/implements predominantly used to create them, to be seized, forfeited or destroyed without compensation.

plain_english_summary: Sets out the core civil remedies for patent infringement in India — injunction plus a plaintiff's choice between damages and an account of profits, plus seizure/destruction of infringing goods, directly comparable to remedies under the Copyright/Trade Marks Acts.

title: Right of exclusive licensee to take proceedings against infringement
text: (1) An exclusive licensee has the same right as the patentee to sue for infringement committed after the licence date; the court considers the exclusive licensee's own losses/profits in awarding relief.

sub_structure.2: (2) The patentee must be joined as defendant (unless already a plaintiff), but is not liable for costs unless they actively participate.

plain_english_summary: Gives an exclusive licensee (not just the patent owner) independent standing to sue infringers — important for a startup holding an exclusive licence to a third party's patented technology, which can enforce that exclusivity directly.

title: Right of licensee under section 84 to take proceedings against infringement
text: A compulsory (section 84) licensee may call on the patentee to sue an infringer; if the patentee refuses/neglects within two months, the licensee may sue in their own name, joining the patentee as defendant (who is not liable for costs unless they participate).
plain_english_summary: Gives a compulsory licensee a fallback right to enforce the patent themselves if the patentee won't act — ensuring compulsory licences remain practically valuable even against infringers.

title: Restriction on power of court to grant damages or account of profits for infringement
text: (1) No damages/account of profits where the defendant proves they were unaware, with no reasonable grounds to believe, that the patent existed at the time of infringement.

sub_structure.1_explanation: Explanation: merely marking an article 'patent'/'patented' does not establish awareness unless the actual patent number accompanies the marking.
sub_structure.2: (2) The court may refuse damages/account of profits for infringement during a period when a renewal fee was unpaid (before any extension).
sub_structure.3: (3) Where a specification was amended (disclaimer/correction/explanation) after publication, no damages/account of profits for use before the amendment decision, unless the original specification was framed in good faith with reasonable skill/knowledge.

plain_english_summary: An 'innocent infringer' defence limiting monetary relief (though not injunctive relief, per sub-section (4)) where the defendant genuinely didn't know of the patent — and notably requires the actual patent NUMBER (not just the word 'patented') to be marked on products to defeat this defence, a practical compliance point for patent marking practices.

title: Certificate of validity of specification and costs of subsequent suits for infringement thereof
text: (1) If a claim's validity is contested and upheld in revocation proceedings before the Appellate Board/High Court, that tribunal may certify the claim's validity was contested and upheld.

sub_structure.2: (2) In later suits/proceedings involving that same claim, a party relying on the certified claim who wins is entitled to full costs, unless the court otherwise directs (subject to a good-faith proviso for parties unaware of the certificate).

plain_english_summary: Creates a 'certificate of validity' that gives a patentee a strong costs advantage in future litigation over the same claim once its validity has already been tested and upheld once — discourages repeat validity challenges on the same claim.

title: Relief for infringement of partially valid specification
text: (1) If some claims are valid (and infringed) while others are invalid, the court may grant relief for the valid, infringed claims — but ordinarily only by way of injunction, not damages/account of profits, unless sub-section (2) applies.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where the plaintiff proves the invalid claim was included in good faith with reasonable skill/knowledge, the court may grant full relief (including damages) on the valid claims, considering the parties' conduct regarding the invalid claim.

plain_english_summary: Addresses the common scenario of a patent with a mix of valid and invalid claims — infringement of the valid claims can still be relieved, though monetary relief is curtailed unless the defective claims were included in good faith.

title: Scientific advisers
text: (1) In any infringement suit or Patent Act proceeding, the court may appoint an independent scientific adviser to assist, or to inquire and report on questions of fact/opinion (not legal interpretation).

sub_structure.2: (2) The adviser's remuneration (fixed by the court, including a daily attendance fee) is paid from Parliament-appropriated funds.

plain_english_summary: Allows courts to bring in independent technical experts in patent litigation — highly relevant to complex software/algorithmic patent disputes where judges need specialist technical input to assess infringement or validity.

title: Appellate Board
text: (1) The Appellate Board established under section 83 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 shall be the Appellate Board for purposes of this Act, exercising the jurisdiction/power/authority conferred by this Act — the Technical Member must meet the qualifications in sub-section (2).

sub_structure.2: (2) A Technical Member must have either at least five years as Controller/exercising Controller functions, or at least ten years as a Registered Patent Agent plus an engineering/technology degree or science master's degree.

plain_english_summary: Establishes the (now-defunct) Intellectual Property Appellate Board as the specialist patent appeal body, shared with the Trade Marks Act, with defined technical-member qualifications. Note: the Appellate Board (IPAB) referred to here was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and its functions were transferred to the High Court — this section's IPAB-era text is preserved for historical/reference purposes.

title: Staff of Appellate Board
text: (1) The Central Government determines and provides the officers/employees needed to assist the Appellate Board. (2) Their salaries/allowances/service conditions are prescribed. (3) They function under the Chairman's general superintendence.
plain_english_summary: Administrative staffing provisions for the Appellate Board. Note: the Appellate Board (IPAB) referred to here was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and its functions were transferred to the High Court — this section's IPAB-era text is preserved for historical/reference purposes.

title: Appeals to Appellate Board
text: (1) Save as in sub-section (2), no appeal lies from any Central Government decision/order/direction, or Controller act/order implementing it. (2) An appeal lies to the Appellate Board from Controller/Central Government decisions under sections 15,16,17,18,19,20,25(4),28,51,54,57,60,61,63,66,69(3),78,84(1)-(5),85,88,91,92 and 94.

sub_structure.4: (4) Every appeal must be filed within three months of the decision/order/direction (or such further time as the Appellate Board allows).

plain_english_summary: Lists the specific Controller/Government decisions appealable to the Appellate Board (e.g. refusal orders, amendment refusals, compulsory-licence decisions) and the three-month appeal deadline. Note: the Appellate Board (IPAB) referred to here was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and its functions were transferred to the High Court — this section's IPAB-era text is preserved for historical/reference purposes.

title: Procedure and powers of Appellate Board
text: The provisions of sub-sections (2)-(6) of section 84, and sections 87, 92, 95 and 96 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, apply to the Appellate Board's functions under this Act as they apply under the Trade Marks Act.
plain_english_summary: Cross-imports the Trade Marks Act's procedural rules (bench composition, powers, etc.) to govern the Appellate Board's patent-related functions. Note: the Appellate Board (IPAB) referred to here was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and its functions were transferred to the High Court — this section's IPAB-era text is preserved for historical/reference purposes.

title: Bar of jurisdiction of courts, etc.
text: No court or other authority has or may exercise jurisdiction/powers/authority over matters referred to in section 117A(2) or section 117D.
plain_english_summary: An exclusive-jurisdiction clause channelling the listed patent appeal and rectification/revocation matters solely to the Appellate Board, ousting ordinary court jurisdiction over them. Note: the Appellate Board (IPAB) referred to here was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and its functions were transferred to the High Court — this section's IPAB-era text is preserved for historical/reference purposes.

title: Procedure for application for rectification, etc., before Appellate Board
text: (1) A revocation application under section 64, and a register-rectification application under section 71, made to the Appellate Board, shall be in the prescribed form.

sub_structure.2: (2) A certified copy of every Board order/judgment on a patent shall be sent to the Controller, who must give effect to it and, if directed, amend/rectify the register.

plain_english_summary: Sets the procedural form for revocation and rectification applications filed directly with the Appellate Board, and the mechanism for the Controller to implement Board orders on the register. Note: the Appellate Board (IPAB) referred to here was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and its functions were transferred to the High Court — this section's IPAB-era text is preserved for historical/reference purposes.

title: Appearance of Controller in legal proceedings
text: (1) The Controller has the right to appear and be heard in Board proceedings involving register rectification/alteration or patent-office-practice questions, and in certain appeals from his own orders.

sub_structure.2: (2) Unless the Board directs otherwise, the Controller may submit a written statement instead of appearing, which is evidence in the proceeding.

plain_english_summary: Governs when and how the Controller participates in Appellate Board proceedings reviewing his own decisions. Note: the Appellate Board (IPAB) referred to here was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and its functions were transferred to the High Court — this section's IPAB-era text is preserved for historical/reference purposes.

title: Costs of Controller in proceedings before Appellate Board
text: In all Board proceedings under this Act, the Controller's costs are in the Board's discretion, but the Controller cannot be ordered to pay any party's costs.
plain_english_summary: Shields the Controller from adverse costs orders in Appellate Board proceedings, even where the Board disagrees with the Controller's original decision. Note: the Appellate Board (IPAB) referred to here was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and its functions were transferred to the High Court — this section's IPAB-era text is preserved for historical/reference purposes.

title: Transfer of pending proceedings to Appellate Board
text: All pending High Court appeals against Controller orders, and pending revocation (other than on infringement counter-claim) and rectification cases, stand transferred to the Appellate Board from the Central-Government-notified date; the Board may proceed de novo or from the transferred stage.
plain_english_summary: The historical transitional provision (2003) that moved existing patent appeal/revocation/rectification cases from the High Courts to the newly-created Appellate Board. Note: the Appellate Board (IPAB) referred to here was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and its functions were transferred to the High Court — this section's IPAB-era text is preserved for historical/reference purposes.

title: Power of Appellate Board to make rules
text: The Appellate Board may make rules, consistent with this Act, as to the conduct and procedure of all proceedings before it under this Act.
plain_english_summary: Delegated rule-making power letting the Appellate Board set its own procedural rules. Note: the Appellate Board (IPAB) referred to here was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, and its functions were transferred to the High Court — this section's IPAB-era text is preserved for historical/reference purposes.

title: Contravention of secrecy provisions relating to certain inventions
text: If any person fails to comply with a section 35 secrecy direction, or files a foreign patent application in contravention of section 39, they are punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both.
plain_english_summary: Criminal penalty (up to 2 years' imprisonment and/or fine) for breaching defence-secrecy directions or the foreign-filing-licence requirement — relevant to dual-use or defence-adjacent software/deep-tech inventions.

title: Falsification of entries in register, etc.
text: Making or causing a false register entry, a writing falsely purporting to be a copy of a register entry, or knowingly producing/tendering such false writing in evidence, is punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both.
plain_english_summary: Criminalises fraudulent tampering with the patent register or fabricating register-extract evidence.

title: Unauthorised claim of patent rights
text: Falsely representing that an article sold is patented in India, or is the subject of a pending Indian patent application, is punishable with a fine up to one lakh rupees.

sub_structure.explanation_1: Explanation 1: marking an article 'patent'/'patented' (or similar) represents it as patented in India; marking 'patent applied for'/'patent pending' (or similar) represents a pending Indian application.
sub_structure.explanation_2: Explanation 2: such markings are deemed to refer to an Indian patent/application unless accompanied by an indication that the patent was obtained/applied for in another country.

plain_english_summary: Criminalises 'patent bluffing' — falsely marking a product as patented (or patent-pending) in India — directly relevant to software/hardware product labelling and marketing claims; penalty is a fine up to Rs 1 lakh.

title: Wrongful use of words "patent office"
text: Using the words "patent office" (or similar words implying official connection to the patent office) on a place of business or issued document, is punishable with imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both.
plain_english_summary: Prevents private entities from misleadingly branding themselves as officially connected to the Patent Office.
keywords: wrongful use of patent office name

title: Refusal or failure to supply information
text: (1) Refusing/failing to furnish information required under section 100(5) (to Central Government) or section 146 (to the Controller, re: working of patents) is punishable with a fine up to ten lakh rupees.

sub_structure.2: (2) Knowingly or believingly furnishing false information/statements when required is punishable with imprisonment up to six months, or fine, or both.

plain_english_summary: Backs up the Controller's power to demand 'working of patents' statements (section 146) with a substantial fine (up to Rs 10 lakh) for non-compliance, and imprisonment for knowingly false statements — relevant to a startup-patentee's annual compliance filings.

title: Practice by non-registered patent agents
text: Contravening section 129 (practising as an unregistered patent agent) is punishable with a fine up to one lakh rupees for a first offence, and up to five lakh rupees for a second or subsequent offence.
plain_english_summary: Criminal penalty for unauthorised practice as a patent agent, with escalating fines for repeat offences.

title: Offences by companies
text: (1) Where a company commits an offence under this Act, both the company and every person in charge of/responsible for its business at the time are deemed guilty and liable, unless they prove the offence was without their knowledge and they exercised due diligence.

sub_structure.2: (2) Where the offence was committed with a director/manager/secretary/officer's consent, connivance, or attributable neglect, that individual is also deemed guilty.
sub_structure.explanation: Explanation: 'company' includes any body corporate, firm, or association of individuals; 'director' of a firm means a partner.

plain_english_summary: Standard corporate-criminal-liability provision attributing Patent Act offences to a company's responsible officers, subject to a due-diligence defence — relevant to how a startup's founders/officers could be personally exposed for Chapter XX offences committed by the company.

title: Register of patent agents
text: (1) The Controller maintains a register of patent agents recording names, addresses, and other prescribed particulars of qualified persons under section 126.

sub_structure.2: (2) The register may be kept in electronic form subject to prescribed safeguards.

plain_english_summary: Establishes the official register of patent agents — India's equivalent of a registered patent attorney roll.

title: Qualifications for registration as patent agents
text: (1) To register as a patent agent, a person must: (a) be an Indian citizen; (b) be at least 21; (c) hold a science/engineering/technology degree (or equivalent), plus either pass the qualifying examination, or have 10+ years' experience as an examiner or Controller; and (d) pay the prescribed fee.

sub_structure.2: (2) Persons registered before the Patents (Amendment) Act, 2005 may continue to be (or be re-registered as) patent agents on payment of prescribed fees.

plain_english_summary: Sets India's qualification bar for registered patent agents — a science/engineering/technology degree plus a qualifying exam (or long-standing Patent Office experience) — relevant to who a startup may formally engage to prosecute Indian patent applications.

title: Rights of patent agents
text: Every registered patent agent is entitled to practice before the Controller, and to prepare documents, transact business and discharge such other functions as prescribed, in connection with proceedings before the Controller.
plain_english_summary: Confirms the professional rights/scope of practice of a registered patent agent before the Indian Patent Office.

title: Subscription and verification of certain documents by patent agents
text: (1) Applications and communications to the Controller may be signed by a duly authorised patent agent; if the principal is absent from India, they may be signed/verified on their behalf by an authorised patent agent.
plain_english_summary: Allows a patent agent to sign/verify filings on behalf of an applicant, including one located outside India — relevant to foreign-headquartered software companies filing Indian patents through local agents.

title: Restrictions on practice as patent agents
text: (1) No person (alone or in partnership) may practise, describe, or hold themselves out as a patent agent unless registered (and, in partnership, all partners registered). (2) No company/body corporate may practise or hold itself out as a patent agent.

sub_structure.explanation: Explanation: 'practising as a patent agent' includes applying for/obtaining patents, preparing specifications/documents, and giving non-scientific/technical advice on patent validity/infringement.

plain_english_summary: Restricts patent-agent practice to individually registered natural persons (not companies), and defines the scope of regulated 'practice' broadly to include specification drafting and validity/infringement advice.

title: Removal from register of patent agents and restoration
text: (1) The Controller may remove a name from the register, after a hearing and inquiry, where the entry was made by error/misrepresentation/suppression, or the agent was convicted of an offence or found guilty of professional misconduct rendering them unfit.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller may, on application and sufficient cause, restore a removed name to the register.

plain_english_summary: The disciplinary mechanism for removing (and potentially restoring) a patent agent's registration for misconduct or conviction.

title: Power of Controller to refuse to deal with certain agents
text: (1) The Controller may refuse to recognise as agent: an individual removed and not restored; a person convicted under section 123; a non-registered person substantially acting as an agent for their employer's benefit; or a company/firm with such a disqualified person as director/manager/partner.

sub_structure.2: (2) The Controller must refuse to recognise as agent any person who neither resides nor has a place of business in India.

plain_english_summary: Gives the Controller gatekeeping power over who may act as agent before the Patent Office, including a mandatory bar on persons/entities without an Indian residence or place of business.

title: Savings in respect of other persons authorised to act as agents
